LESSONS.title: What an inference engine actually does
LESSONS.goal: Explain what happens between sending a prompt and seeing an answer, and which part of that work an inference engine does.
LESSONS.recall: What do you think happens between sending a prompt and seeing the first word?
LESSONS.predict: If two companies serve identical weights, must their speed and running cost be identical?
example: Your team makes three changes to a chatbot. Which part of the system does each change touch?

First the team fine-tunes the model so its replies follow your house style. That changes the learned weights, or a learned adapter on top of them. It belongs to the model, because the same input can now produce a different prediction.
Next the team has the computer process several people’s questions together. The weights can stay exactly as they were. This is an engine decision about how the work is scheduled and executed.

Finally the team adds a sign-in page and sends each request to whichever machine is free. Those jobs belong to the surrounding service. When the chatbot feels slow, knowing which of the three parts changed tells you where to start looking.

questions.prompt: Two teams use exactly the same learned model weights. Could their engines still take different amounts of time and memory to answer?
options: No. Matching weights force identical execution costs.
Yes. The software can organize and execute the same calculations differently.
Only if one team retrains the model.
questions.why: Fixing the learned numbers leaves open how requests are grouped, how memory is managed and how each calculation runs. One engine may avoid repeated work that another engine performs.
questions.hint: Separate learned numbers from how they are executed.
option_feedback: Weights fix what is computed. How requests are grouped, how memory is managed and which kernels run are separate choices.
Correct: the same calculations can be scheduled, batched and executed in different ways, at different cost.
Retraining changes the weights, but the question holds them fixed, and execution cost can still differ.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s public release supports offline inference. What follows?
options: It is already a complete hosted chat service
It cannot allocate any KV memory
A service still needs surrounding components
questions.why: Offline execution keeps local KV state for each request. A hosted service would still need a distributed cache, online routing and the other pieces the README places outside the release.
questions.hint: Local attention state and a fleet cache system are different things.
option_feedback: A hosted chat service also needs routing, sign-in and streaming, which the release leaves out.
Local KV memory is part of running attention at all; what the release omits is a fleet-wide KV-cache service.
Correct: the release covers execution, so routing, a shared cache service and the rest of a service must come from elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Before you accept an optimization, what should you specify first?
options: Workload, output contract and target metrics
Only a single impressive tokens/s number
questions.why: You need to know what must stay correct and which measured behavior should improve, on a stated workload.
questions.hint: Ask: faster for whom, doing what?
option_feedback: Correct: an optimization only means something against a workload, a statement of which outputs stay legal, and a target metric.
High utilization can coexist with slow responses or wrong outputs, so it says nothing about the contract.
A single throughput figure omits the workload, the latency each user sees and whether outputs stayed correct.

transfer: A friend asks: “If the model has already been trained, why do we still need an inference engine?” Explain the difference, then name one job the surrounding service does.
Names weights and execution separately
Explains iterative next-token prediction
Names one surrounding service responsibility

Training produced the weights, the learned numbers that determine the model’s calculations. Answering repeats one loop. The engine runs those calculations, chooses a next token, appends it to the text so far and goes again. Along the way it manages memory and coordinates the many requests sharing the hardware. The surrounding service has its own jobs, such as signing users in and sending each request to an available machine.
LESSONS.takeaway: The learned model decides which calculations to do. The engine decides how the computer runs them.

activity.title: Put each change in the right place.
activity.intro: A chatbot team makes the three changes below. Decide which part of the system each one mainly belongs to. All three parts sit inside the same visible product.

fields.label: Fine-tune the learned numbers so replies follow your style.
fields.why: Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers or an adapter that changes the model’s predictions.

fields.label: Process several users’ requests together on one accelerator.
fields.why: Grouping requests changes how the calculations are organized and executed. The learned numbers can stay the same.

fields.label: Send a signed-in user’s request to an available machine.
fields.why: Choosing a machine and handling user access are responsibilities of the service around the engine.

activity.conclusion: When something goes wrong, these boundaries tell you where to look first. Model changes alter the predictions. Engine and service changes alter how those predictions are computed and delivered.

LESSONS.example_title: Three changes. Which part owns each one?

visual.title: Model → engine → service
visual.caption: An authored example. These are three responsibilities in one system; a change in one can affect the others.

nodes.label: Model: change the learned behavior
nodes.detail: Fine-tuning changes weights or an adapter. The same input can produce different predictions.

nodes.label: Engine: change how work runs
nodes.detail: Batching combines requests on the computer. Compare predictions to check that the scheduling change preserves the intended behavior.

nodes.label: Service: get the request to a machine
nodes.detail: Sign-in, routing and availability surround model execution. A delay here also affects the user’s wait.

levels.1:
You send a message to a chatbot. There is a pause, and then the answer appears a few words at a time. Somewhere a computer is turning your message into that answer, and a different service running what looks like the same model may do it faster or more cheaply.

To see why, pull apart three things that people often lump together as “the model”: the learned model itself, the software that runs it, and the service you actually talk to.

During training, a computer adjusts a very large collection of numbers until the model gets better at predicting text. Those numbers are the model’s weights. You can think of them as the settings of an enormous machine. Their values decide how information flows through it and which predictions come out.

Training ends with the weights saved to files. Fine-tuning a base model changes those numbers, or adds a smaller learned update on top of them, and so changes how the model behaves.

When the model answers, it uses its weights to score which piece of text could come next. It picks one piece, appends it to the text so far, and makes the next prediction from the longer text. A response is that loop, repeated until it stops.

Running a trained model to make predictions is called inference. In ordinary inference the weights stay fixed. The model’s working state grows as the conversation grows, yet nothing it learned is updated after each word.

Something has to load the weights, reserve memory, decide which requests to work on together, run the calculations and keep track of every unfinished answer. That software is an inference engine. Two engines can run identical weights and still differ in how much memory they use and how long they take.

The service around the engine signs you in and picks which machine receives your request. It also streams the answer back to your screen. Each of those steps adds its own delay, so a fast engine behind a slow service still feels slow.

DeepInfer, the engine DeepSeek has released publicly, is the case study for the rest of the course. Its choices about memory, batching and kernels make more sense once the smaller pieces are in place.
levels.2:
Follow a single request through the system. The text first becomes a sequence of numbered pieces called tokens. The engine runs those numbers through the model’s calculations and gets back a score for every possible next piece. It chooses one, and the process runs again on the longer sequence. Between rounds the answer is unfinished, so the engine has to remember which working state belongs to which request.

That bookkeeping is what makes an engine more than a function that loads a file and returns a paragraph. It coordinates a repeated process for many requests at once, all sharing limited hardware.

The engine’s own territory is execution: loading weights, allocating memory, batching requests, holding attention state, running kernels and sampling the next token. A serving system wraps that with routing, admission control, streaming, failure handling and day-to-day operations.

Model quality and serving quality vary independently. A prompt formatted the wrong way can make good weights look bad, and poor scheduling can make a correct model feel slow.

DeepInfer’s README currently names DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as its model. The public release covers offline inference and leaves a full KV-cache service, production disaggregation and replica load balancing outside it. The engine still keeps local attention caches for each request. What the release omits is the fleet-level service built around them.
levels.3:
Suppose you swap the engine and keep the weights. What should stay the same? That depends on the change. Some changes should reproduce the same numbers exactly. Others keep the probability of each possible output the same while letting any single sampled answer differ. Still others approximate the calculation on purpose to save work. Each is a different promise, and it should be named before anyone measures speed.

Write that contract down first. Given the weights, the tokenizer, the prompt’s token IDs, the attention semantics and the sampling settings, which outputs are legal? Then write down the workload and the service targets you care about.

Much of inference engineering comes down to tracing a bottleneck to a layer you can change, then showing that the change is still correct and that it actually helps. A claim of “faster” means little until it says on which workload and under which quality contract.

LESSONS.title: The math you need, without the fog
LESSONS.goal: Read the small amount of arithmetic and notation that inference explanations rely on.
LESSONS.recall: What is a weight, and what changes during inference?
LESSONS.predict: Does a vector with 4 entries multiplied by a 4×6 matrix produce 4 numbers or 6?
example: A weight table has 10 rows and 20 columns, and each number takes two bytes. How much storage does the table need, and how long does it take to move?
Count the entries first: 10 × 20 = 200 numbers. The shape alone tells you how many values exist, without looking at any of them.
Multiply by the storage per entry: 200 × 2 = 400 bytes. That is the raw numbers only. A program may need more memory for bookkeeping and temporary results.

Now send those 400 bytes over a link rated at 100 bytes per second. Even with no overhead the transfer takes four seconds, because bytes divided by bytes per second leaves seconds. The same reasoning applies later to billions of model weights.

questions.prompt: X has shape [8,4] and W has shape [4,6]. What shape is XW?
questions.why: The shared inner dimension 4 is summed away and the outer dimensions remain, so XW has 8 rows and 6 columns.
questions.hint: Track tokens on rows and output features on columns.
option_feedback: Correct: the shared inner dimension 4 is summed away, leaving the 8 rows of X and the 6 columns of W.
This keeps the inner dimension, which is exactly the one the multiplication combines.
[6,8] is the shape of the transpose, (XW)ᵀ. XW keeps the rows of X first.

questions.prompt: A billion parameters at 2 bytes each need roughly how much memory?
options: 2 GB for the entire service including every cache
questions.why: Parameter count times bytes per parameter gives the storage for the weights. The running footprint also includes caches, activations and runtime overhead.
questions.hint: What memory has the calculation omitted?
option_feedback: Off by a factor of a thousand: 10⁹ × 2 bytes is 2 × 10⁹ bytes, while 2 MB is 2 × 10⁶ bytes.
Correct: 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 2 × 10⁹ bytes, about 2 GB, and that covers the weights only.
The arithmetic gives 2 GB, but it counts weights only. Caches and working memory come on top.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many FLOPs does multiplying a 4×6 matrix by a 6×5 matrix take?
questions.why: The product has 4 × 5 = 20 entries, each built from 6 multiply-add terms. Counting multiplications and additions separately gives 2 × 4 × 6 × 5 = 240.
questions.hint: Each of 20 outputs has 6 multiply-add terms.
option_feedback: 120 counts each multiply-add once. Counting the multiplication and the addition separately doubles it.
Correct: 20 outputs each need 6 multiplications and 6 additions, so 2 × 4 × 6 × 5 = 240.
24 multiplies only two of the dimensions and ignores the 6 terms summed for each of the 20 outputs.

transfer: Explain the difference between how much memory a device has and how quickly it can move data. Use a small example.
Separates capacity from transfer rate
Names bytes/s as bandwidth
Explains why both constrain inference

Capacity is how much data fits at once. Bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second. A table of 200 numbers at two bytes each needs 400 bytes of raw storage. Over a link that moves 100 bytes per second, moving it takes at least four seconds. Having room to store the table does nothing to make that transfer faster.
LESSONS.takeaway: A tensor’s shape tells you how its numbers are arranged. The units tell you what a calculation measures.

levels.1:
Explanations of inference tend to jump straight to words like “tensor” and “matrix multiplication”. The ideas underneath are concrete enough to work through on paper, so that is where to start.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [2, 3]. A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers, with rows and columns. Tensor is the general name for an array organized along any number of directions. A vector has one direction and a matrix has two.

Suppose you have four requests, each ten text positions long, and you represent every position with six numbers. You can store all of it in a tensor of shape [4, 10, 6]. The shape records how many requests, positions and features there are. It says nothing about the values stored inside.

That gap matters when you debug. Two tensors can share a shape and hold completely different values, so a passing shape check rules out some mistakes and proves nothing about whether the model computed the right answer.

The expression [2, 3] · [4, 5] asks you to multiply matching entries and add the results: 2 × 4 + 3 × 5 = 23. That is a dot product. Matrix multiplication performs many dot products at once, and inside a model a learned matrix uses them to turn one set of features into another.

Papers write shapes with symbols such as [B, d], where B might be the number of positions being processed and d the number of features per position. Multiplying by a matrix of shape [d, h] gives [B, h]. The shared d is the dimension that gets summed away.

Inference arithmetic also keeps asking how many bytes fit and how long they take to move. If each stored number takes two bytes, a billion numbers take about two billion bytes, which is two decimal gigabytes. That covers those numbers only. Any other working memory comes on top.

A device that moves one hundred gigabytes per second needs at least a hundredth of a second, ten milliseconds, to move one gigabyte. Capacity is about what fits and bandwidth is about how fast it moves. Later lessons use that difference to explain why very fast hardware sometimes spends its time waiting.
levels.2:
When you meet a matrix formula, ask what each row represents, what each column represents and which dimension is combined. Only then do the arithmetic. To estimate work, count one multiplication plus one addition as two floating-point operations. That is accurate enough without following every instruction the hardware runs.

A library may store a matrix in a different orientation from a paper’s notation. Check the declared input and output dimensions instead of assuming every weight matrix is laid out the same way.

With row vectors, x[1,d] × W[d,h] = y[1,h]. For B tokens, X[B,d] × W[d,h] = Y[B,h]. Each output entry takes about d multiplications and d additions, so the whole product costs about 2Bdh FLOPs.

A FLOP is one floating-point operation, and FLOP/s is a rate of them. GB means 10⁹ bytes, while GiB means 2³⁰ bytes. Capacity is measured in bytes and bandwidth in bytes per second. Mixing these units up is a common source of bad hardware estimates.

Logarithms turn products into sums: log(p₁p₂)=log p₁+log p₂. That is why a model’s surprise at a known stretch of text is reported as the average negative log probability of its target tokens.
levels.3:
Some symbols count work and others describe a rate. Dividing FLOPs by FLOP/s gives seconds, and so does dividing bytes by bytes per second. If the units in a calculation do not cancel to the quantity you want, stop before trusting the number.

Check dimensions before doing algebra. If W maps d input features to h output features, how it is stored depends on the library. PyTorch’s linear layers store it as [h,d] and apply the transpose to row-vector inputs.

A gradient tells training how changing a parameter would change the loss. Inference usually turns gradient tracking off, so it needs neither the activations saved for a backward pass nor optimizer state. Estimating inference memory with a training multiplier would overcount it.

Stable softmax subtracts the largest logit before exponentiating. The result is mathematically identical, and the intermediate values no longer overflow. Engines contain many rewrites of this kind, which change the order or representation of operations while keeping the math the same.

LESSONS.title: Tokens, logits and choosing what comes next
LESSONS.goal: Follow the repeated choices that turn a prompt into a generated response.
LESSONS.recall: How is a probability different from an arbitrary numerical score?
LESSONS.predict: If you raise temperature, do you add knowledge or change how the same scores are sampled?
example: The model gives three possible next tokens probabilities of 66.5%, 24.5% and 9%. What happens next?
Under greedy decoding the engine picks the first token, because 66.5% is the largest probability. No random draw is needed.

Under sampling the first token is still the most likely, but either of the others can be drawn. Seeing the second token, which has a 24.5% chance, is no evidence on its own that the engine made a mistake.

Whichever token is chosen joins the sequence, and the next prediction uses the updated sequence. Raising the temperature would reshape the distribution for this choice and leave the learned weights untouched.

questions.prompt: What does temperature change?
questions.why: Temperature rescales the logits at sampling time, after the model has computed them. The weights and the vocabulary stay as they were.
questions.hint: Which part happens after the model computes its scores?
option_feedback: Temperature is applied after the model has produced its scores, and the weights that produced them stay fixed.
Correct: dividing the logits by T reshapes the probabilities used to pick the next token.
The vocabulary is fixed by the tokenizer. Temperature only changes how likely each existing token is to be picked.

questions.prompt: Why can’t ordinary autoregressive generation choose 100 unknown future tokens independently in one step?
options: All GPUs forbid matrices with 100 rows
questions.why: Each future conditional distribution depends on the tokens generated before it. Speculative decoding works around this by proposing several candidates and then verifying them.
questions.hint: Known text and unknown text have different dependencies.
option_feedback: Correct: the distribution for each token depends on which tokens were chosen before it, so later choices cannot be made first.
GPUs routinely multiply matrices with far more than 100 rows. The limit comes from the dependency between tokens.
Tokenization is deterministic for a given tokenizer. Randomness enters only at sampling.

questions.prompt: Two engines diverge on the 20th generated token. A useful next check is…
options: Teacher-force the same prefixes and compare logits
Increase temperature until the text looks similar
questions.why: Once two outputs diverge, every later token is conditioned on a different history. Teacher forcing keeps the history identical, so any remaining difference in logits comes from the computation itself.
questions.hint: Keep the input to the comparison identical.
option_feedback: The final paragraphs mix every earlier difference together and cannot show where the first disagreement began.
Correct: feeding both engines the same prefixes lets you compare their scores before different histories confound the comparison.
Raising temperature buries the disagreement under more randomness and makes the outputs harder to compare.

transfer: Explain how a model goes from a prompt to a longer answer. Include where choosing the next token happens.
Describes turning text into token IDs
Explains scoring, choosing, and appending a next token
Explains why the chosen token affects the next prediction

The tokenizer turns the prompt into token IDs. The model computes a score for every possible next token, and the engine’s selection rule picks one. That token is appended before the next prediction, so each choice shapes the input to the next step. The tokenizer and stop markers have to match what the model was trained with. Changing temperature changes which tokens get picked, while the learned weights stay the same.
LESSONS.takeaway: Generation repeatedly scores possible next tokens, chooses one, and adds it to the text so far.

levels.1:
Before the model runs, a piece of software called the tokenizer breaks your text into smaller pieces and gives each one an integer. The pieces are tokens and the integers are token IDs.

A token can be a common word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a special marker. An invented tokenizer might split “unhelpful” into “un”, “help” and “ful”. Real tokenizers each make their own choices, and the split for any given word depends on which one you use.

So a limit of a thousand tokens is a different limit from a thousand words. It is also why a fine-tuned model has to be loaded with its own tokenizer, since its weights were learned against those particular token IDs.

Suppose the input ends with “The sky is”. The model produces a score for every token it could place next, and some continuations score far higher than others. These raw scores are called logits. They are not probabilities yet, and they need not add up to one.

A function called softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Each probability says how likely one choice is, and across all the candidate tokens they sum to one.

The engine still has to pick. It can take the highest-scoring token every time, which is called greedy decoding. Or it can draw a token at random according to the probabilities, in which case a less likely token is sometimes chosen, just as a coin that lands heads 70% of the time still lands tails now and then.

Temperature controls how concentrated those probabilities are. A low temperature gives the top choices more of the probability, and a high temperature spreads it out. Either way the model’s knowledge is untouched. Only the rule for choosing has changed.

Once a token is chosen, the engine appends it to the sequence and the model scores what could follow the longer text. Choosing “blue” puts the model in a different situation from choosing “clear”, so every later prediction can differ.

The engine repeats this cycle of scoring, choosing and appending until it reaches a stopping condition. The answer on your screen is the trail of those choices, assembled one token at a time.
levels.2:
In the formula below, z stands for the raw scores and T for the temperature. Dividing by a small positive T stretches the gaps between scores before softmax turns them into probabilities. The denominator sums the exponentials of every candidate’s score, which is what makes the probabilities add to one.

Knowing which parts are fixed matters more than memorizing the formula. The scores come from the model. Temperature and any filtering of candidates belong to the selection step.

For logits z and temperature T > 0, pᵢ=exp(zᵢ/T)/Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T). As T shrinks, probability concentrates on the top score. Greedy decoding is the limit of that process, the argmax, and engines usually implement it as a separate branch.

Top-k keeps the k highest-scoring candidates. Top-p sorts the candidates and keeps the shortest prefix whose probabilities add up to at least p. The order in which filtering and temperature are applied changes the result, so record the engine’s actual configuration whenever you compare outputs. DeepInfer keeps these steps in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sampler.py, alongside verification, residual resampling and grammar masks.

A causal model factors a sequence’s probability as P(x₁…xₙ)=ΠₜP(xₜ|x<ₜ). The prompt’s tokens are already known, so the engine can evaluate them together. Each generated token depends on the choices before it and has to wait its turn.
levels.3:
Giving two engines the same visible question is not enough to compare them if they turn it into different token IDs. Hugging Face’s chat-templating documentation treats the prompt format as part of what the model was trained on, and a mismatched template changes the IDs. Even with matching IDs, a different sampling rule can send the continuation somewhere else. A useful debugging comparison pins down both, so you can find the first place where the calculations disagree.

A seed fixes the pseudorandom draws and nothing else. If floating-point reductions run in a different order, the logits can shift slightly. A tiny shift can flip an argmax or a sampled token, and from then on the rest of the sequence diverges.

Teacher forcing feeds the model a known continuation in place of its own outputs. Two generators that would drift apart can then be compared on next-token log probabilities at identical prefixes, which makes it one of the most useful correctness checks an engine developer has.

LESSONS.title: A transformer pass and its KV cache
LESSONS.goal: Explain how a new token uses earlier text, and what the engine remembers to avoid repeating work.
LESSONS.recall: What makes a generated token depend on earlier ones?
LESSONS.predict: If you retain old keys and values, do you still need to compare a new query with them?
example: The prompt contains tokens A, B and C, and the engine is now processing token D. What can it reuse?
The engine already holds keys and values for A, B and C at every layer. They stay in this request’s cache, and D’s arrival is no reason to rebuild them.

Compute D’s query, key and value. D’s query is compared with every visible key, including D’s own, and the matching values are mixed into D’s attention result. The engine reads the earlier cache to do this.

Append D’s key and value so the next position can use them. If the engine reads another request’s cache by mistake, or writes D into the wrong slot, the result can be wrong even though the cache has the expected length.

questions.prompt: What does a KV cache mainly save?
options: Recomputing earlier positions’ keys and values
questions.why: Each new query still attends to the cached context. What the cache saves is rebuilding the earlier positions’ keys and values at every step.
questions.hint: Saved computation does not mean zero reads.
option_feedback: Correct: keys and values for earlier positions are computed once and read again, instead of being recomputed.
Each new query still has to attend over the cached keys and values. The cache saves recomputation, and the reads remain.
The cache holds per-request intermediate results. The weights are still needed to compute every new position.

questions.prompt: Can a text token reuse the same KV vector in any sentence?
options: Yes, keys depend only on spelling
No, hidden states depend on context and position
questions.why: Later-layer representations reflect the preceding tokens and the token’s position, so a key or value is tied to one history.
questions.hint: The token embedding is only the start of the computation.
option_feedback: Spelling fixes only the token’s embedding. Keys and values at later layers depend on the preceding text and the position.
Correct: hidden states reflect the preceding tokens and the position, so the same token gets different keys and values in different contexts.
Temperature affects only how the next token is chosen and has no effect on the keys and values the layers compute.

questions.prompt: Which check most directly tests a KV cache?
options: Full-forward and incremental logits agree on the same prefixes
The cache has the expected Python type
questions.why: Numerical agreement across positions tests the actual computation the cache is meant to reproduce.
questions.hint: Compare a reference computation, not the appearance of the result.
option_feedback: Fluent text can hide a subtly wrong cache, because the model may still produce plausible words from slightly wrong scores.
Correct: if incremental and full-forward logits match at every prefix, the cache reproduces the computation it replaces.
A correct Python type says nothing about whether the stored values are the right ones.

transfer: Walk through what the engine does when one new token arrives. What does it calculate, and what can it reuse?
Computes a new query/key/value
Uses past keys and values
Appends request-specific state

The new position needs its own query, key and value. Its query is compared with the visible keys to decide how to mix the matching values. Keys and values for earlier positions come from this request’s cache and are not recalculated. The engine then appends the new key and value to that cache. It still reads the earlier state on every step, and that state has to come from the correct history.
LESSONS.takeaway: The engine saves earlier attention state so each new token can use it without rebuilding it.

levels.1:
Read “The trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too large.” To decide what “it” refers to, you have to use words elsewhere in the sentence. A model faces the same problem, so it needs a way for the representation at one position to draw on information from other positions.

Attention is the mechanism transformers use for this. The model first represents each token as a list of numbers called an embedding. It then transforms and mixes those lists through a stack of layers, each of which is one stage of the calculation.

At each position, a layer computes three lists of numbers. The query is compared with the keys of every visible position to produce matching scores, and those scores decide how much of each position’s value goes into a weighted mixture. A position with a high score contributes more.

The names sound human, yet nothing is asking a literal question or looking anything up in a dictionary. Queries, keys and values are lists of numbers produced by multiplying by learned matrices. The names describe the role each list plays in the calculation.

A model trained to continue text must never see the token it is supposed to predict. A causal mask enforces this by blocking attention to later positions. As a result, the computation for an earlier position stays the same when a new token is appended.

That stability is an opportunity. Say the engine has processed “The sky is” and is working on the next token. It has already computed keys and values for the earlier positions, so it can keep them in memory and skip computing them again.

The saved state is a KV cache, K for keys and V for values. The new position still needs its own calculations, and its query still reads the saved keys and values. Caching removes repeated work, while the earlier context still has to be read on every step.

“Bank” in a sentence about a river ends up with a different representation from “bank” in a sentence about money, because deeper layers fold in context. A cached key or value therefore cannot in general be reused just because the same token ID shows up somewhere else.

That gives the engine a concrete job. It has to keep the right state for each request, use it in the right order and release it once it is no longer needed. Get this wrong and the predictions can be wrong while every array still has a perfectly valid shape.
levels.2:
The attention equation below compresses that compare-and-mix process. Multiplying the queries by the transposed keys gives one score for every visible query–key pair. Softmax turns the scores into mixture weights, and multiplying by the values produces the mixed representation.

During the first pass over a prompt, many queries are known at once. During generation, one new query arrives each time the sequence grows. With saved keys and values, both paths compute the same causal function without redoing the earlier work.

For one head, Q=XWq; K=XWk; V=XWv, then A=softmax(QKᵀ/√d + causal_mask)V. Multiple heads apply different learned projections in parallel. A residual connection adds a layer’s input back to its output, and normalization keeps the scale of the numbers stable. The Transformer chapter of Google DeepMind’s Scaling Book works through the matrix shapes involved.

Prefill computes many positions under a triangular mask. Decode computes one new position, appends its K and V, and attends over the prefix. A cache entry depends on the layer, the position and everything that came before it, so a text token alone does not identify a reusable KV value.

Cache state therefore belongs to one request running on one particular model. It is never global to a token ID.
levels.3:
The most useful first test of a cache computes the same thing two ways. One path recomputes the whole prefix from scratch. The other processes it incrementally, saving K and V as it goes. Compare their numerical outputs at every position. A disagreement is an execution bug, and you can chase it before anyone judges whether the generated prose reads well.

With conventional full attention, the cache avoids recomputing the prefix’s projections and feed-forward work. Attention for each new query still grows with the length of the visible prefix. A KV cache spends memory capacity and bandwidth to save that recomputation.

Run the comparison at every position, including right after a long prefill. Then interleave two independent requests, because a cache that is accidentally shared between requests can pass every single-request test.

The course’s CPU workshop builds a tiny but real causal attention block. It leaves out production positional schemes, multiple heads and normalization so that the cache mechanism stays easy to inspect.

LESSONS.title: Prefill, decode and what users feel
LESSONS.goal: Separate the wait before an answer starts from the speed at which it continues.
LESSONS.recall: Why are known prompt tokens different from unknown generated tokens?
LESSONS.predict: A huge prompt gives a long initial pause but fast streaming. Which phase should you investigate first?
example: The first token arrives after 400 milliseconds. Nine more tokens arrive with 50 milliseconds between them. When is the answer complete?
The first token arrives at 400 milliseconds, and that wait is counted once. Depending on where the clock started, it may include queueing, input preparation and model execution.
Nine gaps follow the first token. Nine times 50 milliseconds is 450 milliseconds, all of it spent continuing the answer.
Add the two parts: 400 + 450 = 850 milliseconds. Shortening the initial wait and shortening every later gap change different parts of that total.

questions.prompt: An answer begins after a long pause and then streams quickly. Which metric should you look at first?
questions.why: The symptom concerns the time until the first token, so TTFT is the measurement that matches it. The quick streaming suggests decode is not the problem.
questions.hint: Match the metric to the experience.
option_feedback: Correct: the symptom is the wait before the first token, which is exactly what TTFT measures.
The token count says how long the answer is, and nothing about when its first token arrived.
Training loss describes how well the model learned. It says nothing about serving delay.

questions.prompt: 100 requests each receive 10 tokens/s. What is the aggregate output rate?
questions.why: Aggregate throughput sums the per-request rates: 100 × 10 = 1,000 tokens/s. Each user still sees only 10 tokens/s.
questions.hint: Per-user and fleet metrics use different denominators.
option_feedback: 10 tokens/s is the per-request rate. The aggregate adds up all 100 requests.
100 tokens/s counts one token per second per request, when each request gets ten.
Correct: 100 requests × 10 tokens/s each = 1,000 tokens/s across the system.

questions.prompt: Offline throughput improves while online p99 worsens. Is that possible?
options: Yes, batching or queueing can raise tail latency
questions.why: An offline benchmark measures total work with every request present from the start. Online, requests arrive over time and may wait to join a batch, so the slowest ones can get slower.
questions.hint: What happens to a request waiting to join work?
option_feedback: Throughput measures total work per second. It does not determine how long any single request waits.
Correct: larger batches can raise total throughput while requests waiting to join them see longer tail latency.
The weights affect what is computed. Scheduling alone can trade tail latency for throughput.

transfer: Someone says their chatbot is slow. What would you ask and measure before choosing a fix?
Separates initial delay and streaming gaps
Includes queueing/preprocessing
Requests workload and percentile measurements

I would first ask whether the delay comes before the first token or between later tokens. The initial wait can include queueing, input preparation and prompt processing. Later gaps point at continued generation, though delivery can matter there too. I would time those stages under the person’s real input lengths and request load, and look at the slow requests as well as the average. That tells me where to start.
LESSONS.takeaway: Processing the known prompt and generating the unknown continuation are different kinds of work.

activity.title: Measure the wait a user actually sees.
activity.intro: A request waits in a queue for 120 milliseconds. Input preparation, prompt processing, and first-token delivery take another 180 milliseconds. The answer contains five output tokens, with 40 milliseconds between successive tokens. Use the moment the request was submitted as time zero.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the first output token arrives?
fields.why: The initial wait includes both the queue and the work before first delivery: 120 + 180 = 300 milliseconds.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the fifth and final output token arrives?
fields.why: After the first token there are four gaps, not five: 300 + 4 × 40 = 460 milliseconds.

activity.conclusion: A timer that runs only inside the engine can miss the queue and the delivery. Whenever you measure your own model, save the clock boundaries along with the number.

levels.1:
You ask a question and wait several seconds before anything appears. Once the answer starts, it pours out. Another service starts answering almost at once and then trickles along. Both get described as “the model is slow”, and the two symptoms usually have different causes.

Inference engines split the work into prefill and decode. Prefill processes text that is already known, which is your prompt. Decode extends the sequence by generating new tokens.

Every prompt token is available before the model starts answering. A well-organized engine can therefore process many prompt positions together, as long as no position reads ahead of itself. This pass builds the attention state that generation will reuse.

The answer tokens do not exist yet. The engine chooses one, feeds it back in to continue the calculation and repeats. That dependency makes decode behave very differently from prefill.

Time to first token (TTFT) is how long the first generated token takes to arrive, measured between whichever start and end points you choose. A high TTFT can come from waiting in a queue, preparing the input, processing the prompt or delivering the result.

Inter-token latency, also called time between tokens, is the gap between successive generated tokens. It describes how smoothly the answer flows once it has begun.

Throughput is the total work completed per second across all requests. A server answering a hundred people can post high throughput while each of them watches a slow answer, so always check whether a number describes one user or the whole system.

If a long document produces a long initial pause and then fast streaming, start with prompt processing and everything before it. If the first token is quick and the rest are slow, look at generation. Queueing and network delays can produce either symptom, so treat these as starting points.

When you evaluate an engine for your own fine-tuned model, record both the initial wait and the streaming speed. A single tokens-per-second figure leaves out half of what the user experiences.
levels.2:
Break a request into timed stages instead of treating it as one opaque duration. A useful timeline has queue wait, input preparation, prefill, the first output and the gaps between later outputs. Note where your clock starts and stops, because a timer inside the engine misses delays that a user in a browser still experiences.

An answer with ten tokens has one initial wait and nine gaps after it. Counting ten gaps would add a delay that never happened.

A useful decomposition is TTFT ≈ queue + preprocessing + prefill + first-sample + delivery. Total generation time is roughly TTFT plus the gaps for the remaining tokens. When prefill and decode share an accelerator, they compete for it.

Continuous batching admits and retires requests between steps instead of waiting for a fixed batch to finish. Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into budgeted pieces so it can share the device with decode more smoothly.

The inference chapter of Google DeepMind’s Scaling Book explains why prefill is often limited by compute and low-batch decode by memory bandwidth. Use that as a first hypothesis. Context length, architecture and load can all change which resource runs out first.
levels.3:
An average can hide the users who wait longest. A percentile such as p99 is the value that 99% of measurements fall at or below. When a service is overloaded, those long waits can grow even while the GPU’s own step time barely moves, which is why the pattern of request arrivals belongs in any online benchmark.

Report p50, p95 and p99 alongside the mean. A benchmark that raises batch size without modelling arrivals cannot characterize an online service on its own.

Goodput needs an explicit definition: the useful completed tokens or requests per second that meet your quality and latency criteria. Exactly what counts is a product decision. Compare configurations at a matched latency constraint, since peak offline throughput says little about what users will see.

LESSONS.title: Why GPUs wait: memory, math and kernels
LESSONS.goal: Explain why an expensive GPU can wait for data instead of doing useful arithmetic.
LESSONS.recall: How do capacity and bandwidth differ?
LESSONS.predict: If weights take 8 ms to read but arithmetic takes 1 ms, will twice the arithmetic speed halve the step?
example: A toy operation reads 8 GB at 1,000 GB per second, and its arithmetic takes 1 millisecond. What is the main limit?
Start with the transfer: 8 GB divided by 1,000 GB per second is 0.008 seconds, or 8 milliseconds. Keeping bytes and bytes per second in matching units makes the answer come out as a time.
Set that beside the 1 millisecond of arithmetic. Even if the two overlap perfectly, the operation takes at least the larger time, 8 milliseconds. Less overlap or extra overhead makes it longer.

Doubling the arithmetic speed turns 1 millisecond into half a millisecond and leaves the 8-millisecond transfer in place. Under these assumptions, cutting data traffic or reusing the fetched data for more work is the more promising direction.

questions.prompt: When do faster math units help least?
questions.why: Speeding up a resource that is not the limit leaves the limiting cost in place. In the 8 ms versus 1 ms example, even infinitely fast arithmetic could save at most that 1 ms.
questions.hint: Compare the two time estimates.
option_feedback: Correct: when moving data takes longer than the arithmetic, faster arithmetic shortens a cost that was not setting the pace.
When arithmetic dominates, faster math units attack exactly the limiting cost, so this is where they help most.
A model’s name has no effect on execution. The answer depends on which resource is the limit.

questions.prompt: What is 8 GB divided by 1 TB per second?
questions.why: With decimal units, 1 TB/s is 1,000 GB/s, so the transfer takes 8 / 1,000 = 0.008 seconds.
questions.hint: A TB is 1,000 GB here.
option_feedback: 8 seconds would need a rate of 1 GB per second, a thousand times slower.
Correct: 1 TB is 1,000 GB, so 8 / 1,000 seconds is 8 milliseconds.
8 microseconds would need a rate of 1,000 TB per second, a thousand times faster.

questions.prompt: Why can fusion help without reducing mathematical FLOPs?
options: It changes all probabilities to zero
It can remove intermediate writes and launch overhead
It trains a smaller model automatically
questions.why: Execution cost includes moving intermediate results through memory and dispatching each kernel. Fusion reduces both while doing the same arithmetic.
questions.hint: Math count is only one budget.
option_feedback: Fusion leaves the mathematical result unchanged. Setting probabilities to zero would change the model’s output.
Correct: a fused kernel keeps intermediates in fast memory and launches once, cutting traffic and dispatch cost.
Fusion is an execution change applied to the existing model. It does no training.

transfer: A teammate suggests using a smaller numerical format to speed up your endpoint. What would you want to know before adopting it?
Identifies limiting operation and resource
Checks hardware/kernel support
Tests numerical/task quality and end-to-end latency

I would first find which operation and which resource are taking the time. Storing fewer bytes helps when data movement is the limit, and it does nothing for a scheduling delay or a slow conversion step. I would check that the hardware and kernels support the format, compare outputs with a reference and evaluate task quality. Then I would rerun the same workload to see whether the latency users see actually improves.
LESSONS.takeaway: Execution time can be limited by moving data, doing arithmetic, or coordinating the work.

activity.title: Choose which limit to investigate first.
activity.intro: For one toy operation, the amount of arithmetic divided by the arithmetic rate gives 2 milliseconds. Moving the needed data at the available bandwidth gives 8 milliseconds. Assume ideal overlap between the two. This is an estimate for one operation, not a measured whole-model latency.

fields.label: What is the ideal lower bound in milliseconds?
fields.why: With ideal overlap, the lower bound is the larger cost: max(2, 8) = 8 milliseconds.

fields.label: Which limit dominates this estimate?
options: The rate at which data can move
fields.why: The data movement takes longer than the arithmetic under these assumptions. Faster arithmetic alone would leave the 8-millisecond limit.

fields.label: Which observation would best test whether that estimate describes a real run?
options: Only the advertised peak arithmetic rate
A runtime trace showing where time and data movement go
fields.why: A trace can expose actual waiting, transfers, and execution. The toy estimate is a hypothesis about the limiting resource, not evidence that a real run reaches that limit.

activity.conclusion: A simple estimate tells you what to ask the profiler. The observed execution should decide which change you try.

levels.1:
A GPU is a processor built to perform many numerical operations in parallel. Language models are mostly arithmetic, so GPUs suit them well. Its arithmetic units still cannot work on numbers that have not reached them yet.

Model weights and working state live in memory. During execution the data has to travel from that memory to the units doing the calculation, and some results have to travel back. That movement takes time.

Memory capacity is how much data fits. Memory bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second. A model can fit comfortably in memory and still run slowly because every step has to move a lot of data.

You will often see HBM, short for high-bandwidth memory, which is the GPU’s large main memory. Smaller and much faster storage sits closer to the arithmetic units. Much of an engine developer’s work goes into arranging calculations so the data they need is already close by.

Picture an operation that needs eight milliseconds to fetch its data and only one millisecond to do its arithmetic. Doubling the arithmetic speed leaves the eight-millisecond transfer exactly where it was. Data movement sets this operation’s pace.

Now group enough work together that the same fetched weights get used many times. Each byte moved then supports more arithmetic, and the arithmetic units stay busier until some other cost becomes the limit.

Underneath, an engine runs kernels, the programs that carry out individual GPU operations. A better kernel might avoid writing an intermediate result out to slow memory, lay data out more efficiently, or merge several small operations into one.

Storing each number in fewer bytes can also help. That is one purpose of quantization, which represents values in a more limited format. It brings its own questions about rounding, model quality and whether the hardware has an efficient implementation.

So when someone says an optimization makes inference faster, ask which cost it removes, and then check whether that cost dominates your workload. Saving memory capacity and cutting execution time are related, and they are measured differently.
levels.2:
A roofline calculation, which the roofline chapter of Google DeepMind’s Scaling Book builds from first principles, compares two limits quickly. Divide the arithmetic work by the device’s arithmetic rate. Separately, divide the bytes that must move by the available bandwidth. Even with perfect overlap, the operation cannot finish before the larger of the two times.

The result is a lower bound under stated assumptions. Kernel launches, communication, temporary results and imperfect scheduling can all make a real GPU slower.

With ideal overlap, time ≥ max(FLOPs / compute_rate, bytes / bandwidth). Without overlap the two costs may add. Arithmetic intensity is the number of FLOPs per byte moved, and batching raises it by reusing the same weights across many tokens.

Fusion combines operations to cut launches and intermediate memory traffic. Tiling works on chunks small enough to fit in fast memory. Tri Dao and colleagues’ 2022 FlashAttention paper used tiling to compute exact attention without ever writing the full score matrix to HBM, which sharply reduced attention’s memory traffic.

Quantization stores or computes values in a reduced representation. It can lower both traffic and storage, provided suitable kernels exist and a quality check confirms the model still behaves as before.
levels.3:
A useful optimization report ties an observed delay to a specific resource. A trace showing many small kernels separated by launch gaps points to a different problem from one long kernel that already saturates memory bandwidth. Profile the actual operation before deciding that a new numerical format or more hardware will help.

A roofline bound is an estimate, and real kernels fall short of it. Layouts, occupancy limits, padding and imperfect reuse all cost time. A narrower format will not speed anything up if dequantization or missing kernel support dominates.

For a dense projection, the work per token is about 2P FLOPs for P participating weights. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model has both active and total weights, so a memory estimate built for a dense model can mislead. Profile the real traffic and the batch size each expert sees.

DeepInfer integrates specialized kernel libraries. Judge each one on its actual operator, precision and target hardware. A fast custom kernel is a claim about one operation, and an end-to-end win still has to be measured.

LESSONS.title: Batching and overlapping CPU with GPU work
LESSONS.goal: Explain how serving requests together saves work, and why it can still make someone wait.
LESSONS.recall: Why can reusing the same weights across requests improve arithmetic intensity?
LESSONS.predict: If one request finishes early in a fixed batch, must its slot stay empty?
example: A batch holds a short answer and a long answer. The short one finishes first. What should the engine do with its place?
The finished request needs no more model steps. Its state can be released once nothing still reads it, while the long answer keeps its own separate state.
A fixed batch leaves the short request’s place empty until the whole group finishes. Continuous batching admits a waiting request between steps and gives it fresh state of its own.

Reusing the place raises overall throughput. The newcomer still waited before it was admitted, though, and every step still takes time. Measure those delays before claiming that each user got a faster answer.

questions.prompt: Continuous batching lets the engine…
options: Share one request’s private history with everyone
questions.why: The active group is re-formed between steps, so a waiting request can take the place of one that finished.
questions.hint: Which unit finishes independently?
option_feedback: Batched requests share weights and execution steps, and each keeps its own private history.
Right. The group changes between steps, so a waiting request can fill a finished request’s place.
Every request still needs attention over its own context; batching only groups the work.

questions.prompt: Larger batches always improve individual latency.
options: False: step duration and waiting may increase
questions.why: More work per step can raise aggregate throughput while slowing an individual request.
questions.hint: Distinguish amortization from latency.
option_feedback: This mixes up throughput and latency. A bigger batch can make each step take longer.
Right. The total improves, but each step may take longer and a request may wait to join.
Temperature changes how a token is sampled and has no effect on how long a step takes.

questions.prompt: An async rewrite reuses a buffer before its prior output is consumed. Main concern?
options: Data corruption from a lifetime/dependency error
questions.why: Overlapping work changes when memory can safely be reused. If the earlier output has not been read yet, overwriting its buffer corrupts it.
questions.hint: Who still owns a reference to those bytes?
option_feedback: This is a real data race, and a style review would not catch it.
Right. Something still holds a reference to those bytes, so reusing them early can corrupt the result.
Tokenizer size has nothing to do with when a GPU buffer may be reused.

transfer: Explain one useful way for CPU work and GPU work to overlap, and one moment when the engine must still wait.
Shows two execution resources
Names the data dependency causing a wait
Includes startup or draining cost

The CPU can prepare independent metadata for a future step while the GPU calculates the current step, so the GPU does not sit idle afterward. The CPU must still wait before it reads results that have not finished, and it cannot release or overwrite buffers that an unfinished operation still uses. Overlap also has a startup cost before the pipeline fills and a draining cost at the end.
LESSONS.takeaway: Batching spreads execution costs across requests, and the scheduler decides whose work gets those savings and when.

levels.1:
Suppose ten people are using the same model at once. Their questions and conversation histories differ, but every one of them runs through the same weights. An engine can take advantage of that by organizing some of their calculations together instead of running each request from start to finish on its own.

Grouping work this way is called batching. Each weight read from memory now serves several positions, and many small matrix operations merge into a few large ones that keep the GPU’s arithmetic units busy. Fixed costs, such as launching each GPU operation, are spread over more useful work.

The requests still have separate lives. One person asks for a one-line answer; another asks for a long report. If the engine fixes the group at the start and keeps it unchanged until everyone finishes, the short request’s place sits idle while the long one keeps generating.

Continuous batching lets the active group change between execution steps. When a request finishes, a waiting request takes its place on the next step, with its own state. The hardware stays busier, and no request ever has to share another’s conversation.

Deciding what runs in each step is the job of the engine’s scheduler. It has to stay inside memory limits while dividing each step among new prompts, long prompts and answers that are already streaming back to users.

The CPU can also leave the GPU idle. The CPU runs most of the engine’s coordination code: it prepares each step, launches the GPU operations and processes their results. If the GPU finishes a step and then waits while the CPU prepares the next one, arithmetic capacity goes unused.

Some of that preparation can overlap with device work. While the GPU runs one step, the CPU can prepare the parts of a later step that do not depend on results still being computed. Engines call this asynchronous execution. The 2024 NanoFlow paper carries the same idea further, overlapping compute, memory and network work so that no single resource sits waiting on another.

None of this guarantees that a particular request gets faster. A larger batch takes longer per step, and a new request may wait for a free place. Total tokens per second can rise while one user waits longer for the first word of their answer.

A scheduler is making a tradeoff under real demand. To judge one, measure both the useful work completed per second and the waits that individual requests experience.
levels.2:
Picture CPU and GPU work as two lanes on a timeline. Without overlap, the GPU lane sits empty while the CPU lane prepares a step. With overlap, the CPU prepares a future step while the GPU executes the current one. Whether that is allowed depends on whether the preparation needs results that do not exist yet.

Moving independent work earlier is safe. Reading an unfinished result, or reusing memory that an unfinished operation still needs, is not.

Take a serial round that spends 2 ms scheduling, 8 ms executing on the GPU and 1 ms handling results, 11 ms in all. If the CPU work for the next round can run during the current round’s GPU work, the gaps between GPU steps shrink in steady state. The first round still pays its full setup, and the last round still pays to drain.

Asynchronous execution leaves every dependency in place. It moves safe work earlier and waits only at the moment a result is needed. Speculative scheduling adds a further wrinkle: a request may finish, or a draft may be rejected, after the engine has already prepared future work for it, and that work must be discarded cleanly.

DeepInfer describes its async path as “zero-overhead”. The label states a goal. To see what the engine actually overlaps, follow step, _execute_model_async_step and post_process in the engine loop and watch how the worker state changes between them.
levels.3:
A copy that looks wasteful may be protecting the lifetime of data. If an engine returns a view into a reusable buffer, a later step can overwrite that buffer while earlier results still point into it. Before removing a copy, find out who owns the bytes and when every consumer has finished reading them.

Deferred releases, events and pinned host buffers deserve the same suspicion before you delete them. Each one can be enforcing an ordering or a lifetime, so a change to overlap has to preserve command ordering and buffer ownership.

A convincing change comes with a timeline or trace that shows the idle period it removed, plus tests for early stops, cancellations and mixed sequence lengths. GPU utilization alone cannot show which requests benefited.

LESSONS.title: KV memory, paging and prefix reuse
LESSONS.goal: Distinguish keeping a request’s state, organizing its memory and reusing another request’s prefix.
LESSONS.recall: What computation does a KV cache avoid, and what work remains?
LESSONS.predict: If two prompts share the same first 1,000 tokens, can that prefix be reused when their model weights differ?
example: Two requests use the same prompt IDs. The second uses a different adapter that changes attention. Can it reuse the first request’s KV?
The first request’s keys and values came out of its base weights and its adapter. They are numerical results of that particular computation, and the prompt IDs alone do not determine them.

The second adapter can produce different attention state from the same IDs. Reusing the first request’s state would silently mix values from two different models, and the equal tensor shapes would hide the mistake.

Put the model and adapter identity into the cache key, or invalidate the affected state when the adapter changes. To check the fix, alternate the two adapters and compare cached results against uncached reference runs.

questions.prompt: Paging and prefix caching are…
options: Allocation management versus reuse of computed prefixes
questions.why: They can be combined, but they remove different kinds of waste: fragmented memory and repeated prefill.
questions.hint: One asks where state fits; the other asks whether it already exists.
option_feedback: They often work together, yet one decides where state lives and the other decides whether it already exists.
Right. Paging manages where blocks go; prefix caching skips recomputing a beginning that was already processed.
Neither one compresses text. Both handle numerical attention state.

questions.prompt: Double batch and context length, holding all else fixed. Raw KV becomes…
questions.why: Batch and tokens are both multiplicative factors in the conventional cache formula, so 2 × 2 = 4.
questions.hint: Multiply the independent scaling factors.
option_feedback: This counts only one of the two doubled factors.
Right. Batch and tokens are separate multipliers, so doubling both gives 2 × 2 = 4.
Raw state grows with every live position in every request.

questions.prompt: Same token IDs, different LoRA adapter. Reuse old KV by default?
options: No: adapter identity may change cached computation
Yes, if both adapters have the same rank
questions.why: Equal dimensions do not imply equal hidden states. The adapter is one of the inputs that computed the cached keys and values.
questions.hint: What inputs determine the actual keys and values?
option_feedback: The keys and values depend on the weights that computed them, and the adapter is part of those weights.
Right. A different adapter can compute different keys and values for the same IDs.
Matching rank means matching shapes, and matching shapes say nothing about the values.

transfer: A cache finds more matching prefixes, but requests take longer. Give a possible explanation and a measurement that would test it.
Includes transfer or lookup cost
Compares saved computation with added cost
Measures latency, not hit rate alone

Looking up or fetching the saved state may take longer than processing the prefix again. A hit shows that stored work was found; it says nothing about whether fetching it saved time. I would time lookup, transfer and the remaining prompt computation separately for hits and misses, then compare time to first token on a representative workload. I would also check whether the transfers slow down other requests.
LESSONS.takeaway: A cache helps only when it saves the right computation, under a compatible model, and returns it faster than recomputing would.

levels.1:
You have already met the KV cache, the keys and values saved from earlier positions of a request. As the answer grows, so does that saved state. Keeping it spares the engine from recomputing earlier keys and values at every generation step.

Serving many requests at once raises two further questions. How should the engine allocate space for sequences that keep growing? And can a new request reuse work that an earlier request already did?

Start with allocation. If every request needed one large, continuous stretch of memory, requests that grow and finish at different times would leave awkward gaps between them. The engine can instead cut the state into fixed-size blocks and keep a table that maps each request’s logical positions to the blocks it owns.

This is paging, the idea at the center of the 2023 PagedAttention paper that introduced vLLM. It works much like an operating system mapping a program’s virtual pages onto scattered physical memory. Blocks are handed out as a sequence grows, and requests with identical beginnings can point at the same blocks.

Now the repeated work. Suppose thousands of requests begin with the same long system instructions. The engine can keep the saved state for that common beginning and attach it to each new request instead of processing it again. This is prefix caching; a prefix is simply the shared beginning of a sequence. The SGLang paper organizes these saved prefixes in a tree, a design it calls RadixAttention.

The match has to be exact in a specific sense. The text must tokenize to the same IDs, and the model that processes those IDs must perform the same computation. Swap in a different adapter and the keys and values change, even though the prompt text is identical.

A saved prefix also has to be worth fetching. It might live on another machine, and looking it up, transferring it and attaching it to the new request all take time. If recomputing the prefix would have been quicker, a cache hit makes the user wait longer.

Hit rate therefore tells only part of the story. It counts how often stored work was found and says nothing about whether retrieving it made the service faster.

Memory grows with the amount of live context. More requests and longer histories mean more retained attention state. In a conventional cache, doubling both the number of requests and their context lengths makes the raw state four times larger. The exact storage formula depends on the model’s attention design, and compressed designs do not use the conventional layout.
levels.2:
To estimate a conventional cache, count keys and values separately, then multiply by layers, requests, positions, KV heads, the size of each head and the bytes per value. A head is one of the separate attention projections inside a layer. Some architectures let several query heads share one key/value head, which shrinks the retained state.

For an uncompressed cache: bytes = 2 × layers × batch × tokens × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element. The 2 counts K and V. Batch and tokens are separate factors, which is why doubling both quadruples the total.

The formula counts raw entries only. It leaves out temporary working memory, allocator bookkeeping and unused space inside partially filled blocks. It is also not an estimate for DeepSeek V4.1, whose cache uses a different representation.

Grouped-query attention (GQA) lets a group of query heads share one KV head, and multi-query attention goes all the way to a single KV head. These are decisions about the model’s architecture, fixed when the model is designed, and they are separate from how the engine allocates KV pages.

A prefix hit pays off only after four steps succeed: finding the match, retrieving the state, transferring it and attaching it to the request. A slow remote fetch can cost more than the prefill it saves.
levels.3:
Cache correctness is a compatibility problem. A useful test keeps the prompt fixed and switches to an adapter that changes attention. The second request must then behave like an uncached computation under its own adapter, never like a blend of the two models. A test that checks only whether the lookup succeeded would miss this error entirely.

Safe reuse requires matching weights, adapter, tokenization, positional settings, attention semantics and numerical representation. When a conversation adds a new turn, only the longest prefix that is still valid can be reused.

Test the edges: lengths just below, at and above a block boundary, eviction while a request is active, cancellation, and the same prompt under different adapters. Keep allocation bugs, where a request gets the wrong blocks, apart from content bugs, where the right blocks hold the wrong values.

An engine’s local cache allocator and a persistent cache shared across a fleet of machines solve different problems. Check which one a repository actually provides before you plan around it.

LESSONS.title: Compressed attention, sliding windows and replay
LESSONS.goal: Understand what changes when a model compresses, shares or reconstructs its attention state.
LESSONS.recall: Why is the conventional KV formula not universal?
LESSONS.predict: If each layer sees the last 128 tokens, is the entire multi-layer model’s dependence limited to 128 original tokens?
example: An engineer argues that because each layer attends over 128 tokens, replaying the last 128 raw tokens restores a 20-layer model exactly. What is missing?
Take the first token in the replayed region. In the original run, its deeper representations absorbed information that reached it, layer by layer, from positions before the replay boundary.

A replay that starts at the boundary has no access to that upstream state, so it can compute a different deeper representation. The tensors keep their dimensions while the lost information stays lost.

Exactness has to be established separately. Compare the replayed computation with the full reference on identical continuations, including boundary and long-context cases. If an approximation is acceptable, also evaluate the tasks you intend to serve.

questions.prompt: MLA, paging and SWA primarily concern…
options: They all describe the same memory-allocation technique.
They concern what is stored, how memory is organized, and which positions can be read.
They only change how text is split into tokens.
questions.why: Each term answers a different question: what is stored, how memory is organized and which positions can be read. A smaller cache can come from any of them, and each makes a different promise.
questions.hint: Ask a different question for each term.
option_feedback: Only paging is about allocation. MLA changes the representation, and SWA changes visibility.
Right. MLA changes the stored representation, paging organizes memory and SWA limits which positions a query reads.
Tokenization happens before any of these; all three concern attention state.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer bounded SWA replay should be described as…
questions.why: DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A names the reconstruction as approximate. A short window alone cannot make it exact.
questions.hint: Look at the replay boundary’s missing context.
option_feedback: Deeper layers carry information from before the window, so exactness is not automatic, and the Q&A itself calls the path approximate.
Right. The Q&A describes it as an approximate reconstruction of local window state.
Replay rebuilds attention state during inference and has nothing to do with training adapters.

questions.prompt: Mask-vs-compact logprobs agree. This proves…
options: Every approximation in the whole service is exact
Those implementations agree under the tested conditions
questions.why: A comparison proves only the equivalence it states, over the inputs and configuration it tested.
questions.hint: Identify the two things actually compared.
option_feedback: The check compared two implementations of one path, so it says nothing about other approximations.
Right. Agreement holds for those two implementations, under the conditions tested.
Future models may have different dependencies, which this test never exercised.

transfer: Why would you avoid turning on a model-specific cache shortcut for an arbitrary model you fine-tuned?
Names architecture/config dependency
Distinguishes exactness from approximation
Requires reference and task-quality comparison

A shortcut can depend on how one architecture produces and consumes state, and a model I fine-tuned may not share those layer-sharing or attention dependencies. I would first establish compatibility, then find out whether the shortcut promises an exact calculation or accepts an approximation. I would compare it against the appropriate reference, test boundary and long-context cases, and evaluate task quality wherever numerical differences are allowed.
LESSONS.takeaway: A smaller cache can come from a different representation, narrower visibility or an approximation, and each makes a different promise.

levels.1:
So far we have pictured the KV cache as a key and a value saved for every layer and every position. That picture is a good starting point, but model designers are free to change what gets stored and how later layers use it.

Those choices matter to anyone working on an engine. A memory-saving trick that is valid for one architecture can be invalid for another, even when both are called transformers.

Compression changes what is stored. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek’s V2 paper, caches a compressed latent vector for each position, and the layer derives its keys and values from that vector. This changes how the model represents attention information. Paging is a separate matter; it only decides where allocated blocks live.

A window changes what a query can read directly. Sliding-window attention (SWA) limits each position to a recent stretch of the sequence. A layer might let a query read only the last 128 positions, which bounds some of the attention work and some of the stored state.

Layers build on one another, though. A recent position’s representation may already carry information that earlier layers pulled in from older positions. A 128-position window in every layer does not mean the model has forgotten everything more than 128 tokens back.

Sharing changes which layers must do their own work. Some architectures let later layers consume state that earlier layers produced. Yutao Sun and colleagues’ 2024 paper “You Only Cache Once” (YOCO) is the historical background for this kind of design. DeepInfer has its own model-specific producer and consumer layer paths, and their meaning comes from the configuration of the model they support.

Replaying a short segment can be an approximation. DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A describes rebuilding local sliding-window state by replaying a recent 128-token segment with truncated visibility, and it says plainly that the reconstruction is approximate. The replay deliberately skips rebuilding every upstream dependency.

That can be a sound engineering tradeoff, and it raises a specific question: how much does the difference affect the task? Showing that two implementations of the same shortcut agree is a separate result from showing that the shortcut matches the full original computation.

When reading this code, track for each path what is stored, what is reused and what is recomputed. Then pick a numerical or task-level comparison that tests the promise the path actually makes.
levels.2:
Trace a dependency across two layers. In the first layer, a recent token reads an older one. In the second layer, a later token reads that recent token’s updated representation. Information has now travelled farther than either layer’s direct window.

This is the step missing from the argument that replaying one local window must reconstruct all deeper state exactly. An exact bound on replay needs reasoning about the whole dependency path through the architecture.

DeepInfer’s YoCo runtime separates producer and consumer layers according to the model configuration. Its compaction path gathers the retained positions and updates the shared metadata. The code is written for a specific model, and it is not a switch you can flip for arbitrary weights.

The deployment Q&A calls the reconstruction SWA bounded replay: rebuild local SWA state from a recent 128-token segment with truncated visibility. Reusing existing block KV and rebuilding local state are separate actions in that design.

Two claims are easy to blur here. “The mask and compact implementations agree” is one comparison. “Bounded replay equals full exact reconstruction” is another, and the first tells you nothing about the second.
levels.3:
Three kinds of test appear around this code. A metadata check tests retained positions, visible ranges and storage slots. A numerical check compares the values two paths produce along a shared trajectory. A task evaluation measures whether a difference changes useful behavior. Each answers its own question, and none proves more than it actually checks.

An approximation needs a declared reference and a quality budget. Feed the reference and the approximate path the same fixed continuation, compare their log probabilities and task outcomes on representative contexts, and add cases at window boundaries and on long-range dependencies.

DeepInfer’s equivalence-check README separates metadata-level checks from weight-backed log-probability checks. Read its constraints on which checkpoint is compatible before you interpret a pass.

Generic cache intuition is not enough to change this path safely. Before editing it, find the dependency each piece of stored or reconstructed state relies on, and read exactly what its test proves.

LESSONS.title: MoE, parallelism and the slowest worker
LESSONS.goal: Explain what multiple GPUs share, what they split, and why one busy worker can delay the rest.
LESSONS.recall: What is the difference between total parameters and parameters used by one token?
LESSONS.predict: If half the tokens choose experts on one GPU, do equal expert counts guarantee balanced work?
example: Four devices finish their required work in 5, 5, 5 and 15 milliseconds, then synchronize. When can the group continue?
