At 5 milliseconds three devices are ready. Their local work is done, while the fourth device is still computing something the next group operation needs.
The average completion time is 7.5 milliseconds, and the dependency takes no notice of averages. The group continues at 15 milliseconds, when the fourth device finishes.

The next question is why that device is slower. It might have hotter experts, more tokens, slower links or differently sized operations. Moving or replicating the right work could help, while adding devices without finding the cause might change nothing.

questions.prompt: Which scheme puts different experts on different GPUs?
questions.why: Expert parallelism assigns ownership of experts to devices and routes each token to the owners of its chosen experts.
questions.hint: Name the object being split.
option_feedback: Right. EP gives each device its own set of experts and sends tokens to them.
Tensor parallelism splits the matrices of one operation across devices, so every device takes part in every token’s operation.
Temperature changes how tokens are sampled and has nothing to do with where weights live.

questions.prompt: Same number of experts per rank means same execution time.
questions.why: Token demand per expert can be uneven, so ranks with equal expert counts can receive very different amounts of work.
questions.hint: Equal capacity is not equal demand.
option_feedback: Equal counts describe storage. The router decides how much work each expert receives.
Right. If the router favors experts on one rank, that rank does more work and the others wait.
BF16 changes the cost of each operation on every rank alike and leaves the routing imbalance in place.

questions.prompt: Four ranks take 5,5,5,15 ms then synchronize. Phase lower bound?
questions.why: The barrier waits for the slowest required participant, which finishes at 15 ms.
questions.hint: Who has not finished at 7.5 ms?
option_feedback: 7.5 ms is the mean, and at 7.5 ms one rank is still working.
5 ms is when the first three ranks finish; the fourth still has 10 ms to go.
Right. The barrier waits for the slowest rank, which finishes at 15 ms.

transfer: An expert model gets little faster when you double its GPU count. Suggest two possible causes and how you would investigate them.
Includes routing skew or small expert batches
Includes communication/topology
Names a measurement per hypothesis

The router might send a disproportionate share of tokens to a few experts, so some devices finish early and wait. I would measure token demand and execution time per expert and per device. Communication might also grow more expensive as the group grows, especially across slower links between machines, so I would measure those transfers and inspect where the experts are placed.
LESSONS.takeaway: More devices help only when the useful work and the communication between them are organized to benefit.

levels.1:
“Run it on more GPUs” leaves the real design question open. With several devices, you have to decide which one stores which weights and which one does which work, and every choice brings its own communication. Before memorizing the abbreviations, ask what is being divided.

Data parallelism divides independent requests or tokens among devices. Tensor parallelism splits a single numerical operation, such as one large matrix multiplication, across devices. Pipeline parallelism gives different layers to different devices. Context parallelism splits the work on one long sequence. Each name tells you what gets split.

A mixture of experts (MoE) adds another kind of division. The model contains many feed-forward networks called experts, and for each token a router picks a small subset of them. All the experts’ weights exist, but any one token uses only a few.

That reduces the arithmetic per token, yet every expert’s weights still have to be stored somewhere. With expert parallelism (EP), different devices own different experts. Each token travels to the devices that hold its chosen experts, and the results travel back to be combined.

Equal storage does not guarantee equal work. Imagine four devices that each hold the same number of experts. If the router keeps choosing experts on one device, that device receives far more tokens than the others, which finish early and sit waiting for it.

Engine developers therefore measure demand per expert and time per device instead of counting experts. The links between devices matter too, because a fast connection inside one machine behaves very differently from a slower one between machines.

One remedy for a hot expert is to place extra copies of its weights on other devices so they can share the demand. DeepInfer’s expert containers keep the bookkeeping straight by separating logical experts, the learned functions the router selects, from physical placements, which include redundant copies. A copy adds capacity without adding a new learned function.

Copies cost memory and may require weights to be moved between devices. Larger device groups add coordination costs as well. A good design weighs those costs against the waiting it saves.

When you judge a multi-GPU result, start by drawing where the data lives and how it moves. A device count on its own explains very little.
levels.2:
A synchronization point makes a group wait for every required participant. Suppose four devices need 5, 5, 5 and 15 milliseconds. Their mean is 7.5 milliseconds, yet the group cannot pass the barrier until the slowest participant finishes, so the phase takes at least 15 milliseconds.

Load balancing tries to shrink that unevenness. It should be guided by the actual token demand and runtime on each device, since the number of experts assigned to a device says little about either.

Under EP, tokens are routed to the devices that own their experts, processed there and combined. Communication, along with the small per-expert batches that routing produces, can erase the arithmetic savings. Fast links within a node and slower links across nodes behave differently and need to be measured separately.

In DeepInfer’s expert containers, the logical experts that the gate selects are distinct from the physical expert copies. Placement, routing and hot-expert replication together form one load-balancing problem.

DeepInfer’s README lists data-parallel attention with balanced context parallelism, and MoE expert parallelism with an expert-parallel load balancer (EPLB). A list of supported features is a separate thing from a production recipe. The deployment Q&A and the configuration for a particular run show what was actually used.
levels.3:
Spreading weights over more devices reduces the memory each one holds and increases how far tokens travel. Replicating hot weights improves balance and consumes extra memory. Neither wins everywhere. Check the workload, the network topology, the pattern of expert selection and the size of the operations left on each device.

Mean-based arithmetic hides the tail. In the 5, 5, 5 and 15 ms case, moving work off the slow device or replicating its hot expert could bring the phase closer to the 7.5 ms mean, paid for with memory and redistribution traffic.

A larger EP group gathers more tokens for each expert and spreads weight ownership more thinly, while raising synchronization and network demands. Adding GPUs carries no guarantee of speed.

Before reading the benchmark charts for a distributed design, sketch who owns the model state, how tokens move, which collective operations run and what the real link topology looks like.

LESSONS.title: Speculative decoding and DSpark
LESSONS.goal: Explain how guessing several tokens can save time without letting the guesses replace the target model.
LESSONS.recall: What prevents ordinary autoregressive generation from predicting many unknown steps independently?
LESSONS.predict: If draft length doubles, must accepted tokens per second double?
example: Two proposed tokens each have a 50% conditional acceptance rate. How many accepted draft tokens do you expect?
The first token is accepted in half the cases, so it contributes 0.5 tokens on average.

The second token counts only when the first survives and the second then survives too, which happens with probability 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Adding 0.5 for it directly would forget that it needs the first.

Add the contributions: 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 accepted draft tokens on average, before counting the target’s correction or bonus token. Choosing a fast setting still requires the time spent producing and checking the proposals.

questions.prompt: Why verify a draft with the target model?
options: To preserve the target’s intended generation behavior
To avoid loading target weights forever
questions.why: Drafts are proposals. The target remains the reference for what the output should be.
questions.hint: Who decides what output is acceptable?
option_feedback: Right. Verification keeps the output faithful to the target model.
The target’s weights are used in every verification pass, so speculation never retires them.
Speculation happens at inference time and leaves the tokenizer unchanged.

questions.prompt: Two draft positions each survive conditionally with p=0.5. Expected accepted drafts?
questions.why: 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.75. The second position counts only when the first survives.
questions.hint: Accepted prefixes must be contiguous.
option_feedback: This counts each position as 0.5 on its own and ignores that the second needs the first.
Right. 0.5 for the first, plus 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 for the second.
Two is the draft length, which would require both tokens to be accepted every time.

questions.prompt: An exact speculative sampler promises…
options: Identical strings for all hardware and seeds
The target output distribution, assuming the algorithm’s conditions
questions.why: Distributional equality differs from pathwise equality: two valid samples from one distribution can differ.
questions.hint: Think about two valid random samples from the same distribution.
option_feedback: Two valid samples from one distribution can differ, so identical strings are never promised.
Right. The guarantee concerns the distribution of outputs, under the algorithm’s conditions.
The target still evaluates every proposed position, and that costs work.

transfer: Explain how longer drafts could help one user receive tokens faster but reduce the amount of useful work the server does for everyone.
Names saved serial rounds
Names added low-value verification work
Includes concurrency or capacity constraint

A single user may advance through several accepted tokens in one target-model round, which cuts the number of serial waits. Later draft positions have to survive every earlier position, though, so some of the extra checking has little chance of helping. With many requests active, that verification consumes capacity that could serve other users. I would measure accepted progress, drafting and checking time, and latency at the intended concurrency before settling on a draft length.
LESSONS.takeaway: Drafting pays off when the accepted progress is worth more than the work of drafting and verifying it.

levels.1:
In ordinary generation, the model has to choose the next token before it knows the input for the prediction after that. Each round runs the full model, and the rounds happen one after another, so their cost limits how quickly a single person receives an answer.

Speculative decoding, which Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias formalized in 2022, gets more progress out of each round of the main model, called the target. A cheaper drafter proposes several tokens, and the target evaluates all of the proposed positions in a single pass.

The target then checks the proposal. It accepts some draft tokens and corrects the first rejected position. The acceptance rule matters here. Exact speculative sampling, as Leviathan and colleagues define it, preserves the target’s output probability distribution as long as the algorithm’s assumptions hold.

That promise does not mean two implementations will print the same string for the same seed. Two draws from one valid distribution can differ, so matching a distribution and matching one particular random run are different properties.

Later guesses depend on earlier ones surviving. Suppose the drafter proposes three tokens. The third becomes part of the answer only if the first two were accepted as well, so you cannot count each position as if it contributed on its own.

That makes the length of a draft a gamble. A long draft offers a chance to advance far in one round, but its later positions are unlikely to survive, and checking them still uses work that could have served another request.

DeepSeek’s DSpark paper makes that budget choice deliberately. It pairs a draft design with confidence-based verification scheduling. The system estimates how likely each proposed prefix is to survive and weighs that against how its hardware performs at different amounts of verification work.

DeepInfer contains a related scheduling path that turns confidence estimates into a work length for each request. The draft-length experiment here isolates the intuition behind that choice and does not reproduce the full production scheduler.

To evaluate speculation on your own model, measure the useful tokens accepted per round together with the time spent drafting and checking them. A high acceptance rate alone does not prove a speedup, and a setting that helps one user may waste capacity when many users are active.
levels.2:
If the first draft token has an 80% chance of surviving, and the second an 80% chance given that the first survived, both survive with probability 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. The expected number of accepted drafts is the probability that the first survives, plus the probability that the first two survive, and so on. For this two-token draft that is 0.8 + 0.64 = 1.44.

The real acceptance-and-correction rule does more than check whether the target’s favorite token matches the guess. It is built to preserve a sampling distribution.

For exact speculative sampling, a draft token x drawn from the drafter’s distribution q is accepted with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target’s distribution. On rejection, the replacement is sampled from the normalized positive residual max(0,p−q). The full algorithm also handles the accepted prefix and adds one target token when every draft is accepted.

Greedy verification uses a simpler rule: a draft token is accepted when it matches the target’s highest-scoring token.

The DSpark paper balances these prefix survival estimates against a measured hardware throughput profile, because a late token is useful only if every draft token before it survives.
levels.3:
An estimate of accepted length becomes an engineering decision only after you add the cost of verifying that length. Hardware throughput need not grow linearly with the number of proposed tokens, so a practical scheduler uses a measured cost profile and accounts for the target work that must happen whatever the draft contains.

With per-position conditional acceptance probabilities a₁…aₖ, the expected number of accepted drafts is Σᵢ Πⱼ≤ᵢ aⱼ. The formula assumes each probability is conditional on the prefix actually reached, and it leaves out the target’s correction or bonus token.

DeepInfer’s confidence scheduler computes cumulative products, ranks candidate positions across requests and assigns query lengths under a total budget. That kernel is where confidence turns into scheduled work.

Longer drafts and higher acceptance do not automatically raise goodput, the rate of useful output. Measure drafting time, verification cost, accepted output per round and inter-token latency at the concurrency you intend to serve.

LESSONS.title: Correctness, determinism and structured output
LESSONS.goal: Choose a check that tests the specific kind of correctness your change promises.
LESSONS.recall: How does equal output distribution differ from identical outputs?
LESSONS.predict: If JSON parses successfully, have you proved the answer’s facts are true?
example: A cache change produces valid JSON, but its numerical predictions disagree with the reference at a page boundary. Would you accept an exactness claim?
Valid JSON shows that the output followed a structural constraint. It says nothing about whether attention read the right positions or the right cached values.

The disagreement on identical prefixes bears directly on the claimed numerical equivalence. Find the first position and layer where the values differ, starting near the page boundary where the error shows up.

Fix that mismatch before accepting the exactness claim. If an approximation is acceptable instead, state that different contract and test its effect on real task quality. Valid formatting cannot stand in for either check.

questions.prompt: A JSON grammar proves…
options: Conformance to the supported structural constraints
questions.why: Structure and truth are different properties. A grammar constrains form and cannot check facts.
questions.hint: A perfectly formatted wrong answer is still possible.
option_feedback: A grammar constrains form, so a perfectly formatted field can still be false.
Right. The grammar guarantees that the output fits the structure it encodes.
Constrained decoding still samples; the grammar only masks out illegal tokens.

questions.prompt: A seed by itself guarantees batch invariance.
options: No, numerical execution and RNG assignment also matter
questions.why: Different batching can change the order of reductions or which random draw goes to which request, unless both are controlled.
questions.hint: What happens before random selection?
option_feedback: A seed fixes the random draws, yet batching can change the numbers those draws act on.
Right. Batch composition can change reduction order and the assignment of random draws.
Prompt length plays no special role; batch effects can appear at any length.

questions.prompt: Best first oracle for an exact attention-kernel rewrite?
options: Matching layer outputs against a reference over varied shapes
A user says responses feel good
questions.why: Test the numerical claim at the operator boundary before measuring downstream behavior.
questions.hint: Pin the promised invariant directly.
option_feedback: Right. It tests the promised numerical equality directly, across the shapes where bugs hide.
User impressions cannot detect small numerical errors that matter later.
Throughput measures speed and says nothing about whether the outputs are correct.

transfer: Pick an engine change and describe what you would compare to decide whether it is correct. Say what the comparison would and would not establish.
Names a reference
States equality/tolerance/quality criterion
States tested configurations and boundaries

For a cache-read change, I would feed identical token prefixes to the full reference calculation and to the cached path, then compare the next-token scores within a stated tolerance. I would include cache boundaries and interleaved requests. That tests the numerical property directly under those conditions. It does not cover every possible configuration, and it says nothing about whether the model’s answers are factually correct, so those claims need their own checks.
LESSONS.takeaway: A test can pass while the property that matters goes untested. Match each check to the claim it supports.

activity.title: Check the numbers before judging a fluent answer.
activity.intro: Two paths receive the same fixed input IDs [1, 4]. The reference returns next-token scores [0.2, 0.8, -0.1]. A changed path returns [0.2, 0.805, -0.1]. Your stated rule permits an absolute difference of at most 0.001 in every score. Both paths still choose the second token when selecting the highest score.

fields.label: What is the largest absolute score difference?
fields.why: The second entry differs by 0.805 − 0.8 = 0.005. The other entries match.

fields.label: Does the changed path pass the stated numerical rule?
options: Yes, because it chooses the same token
No, because one score difference exceeds the tolerance
fields.why: 0.005 is greater than 0.001. Matching the highest-scoring token does not establish that the numerical comparison passed.

activity.conclusion: A useful correctness check needs fixed inputs, a reference, a comparison rule and a boundary. Passing this one numerical case would still leave request isolation, stop behavior and task quality unchecked.

levels.1:
Suppose you change how a model reads its cache. The program runs, the response sounds fluent and its JSON parses. Has the change preserved the model’s calculation? Each observation is useful, and none of them answers that question.

An array can have the right dimensions and hold the wrong numbers. A paragraph can read well and still differ from what the reference model would have written.

JSON is a structured text format that programs can parse into fields and values. A grammar can restrict which continuations the sampler may choose, so that an answer follows the format. The grammar guarantees structure, and a perfectly formatted field can still hold the wrong date or an invented fact.

Start by naming the property you want to preserve. An exact attention rewrite should match a reference’s numerical outputs within a stated rounding tolerance. An exact sampling method should preserve a probability distribution. A deliberate approximation may differ numerically, as long as task quality stays within an agreed limit.

The trusted comparison path is called a reference, and it is often a simpler implementation. A check that tells you whether the property holds is sometimes called an oracle. The name does not make it infallible, so you still need to understand exactly what it checks.

Control the input when you compare outputs. If two generators pick different tokens, their later inputs differ too, and every difference after that point becomes hard to interpret. Feed both implementations the same known continuation instead, and compare their predictions at the same positions. This is called teacher forcing.

Teacher forcing lets you find the first disagreement before diverging histories bury its cause.

Some bugs never appear in a pleasant example. A cache bug might show up only when a sequence crosses a block boundary. A state leak might need two requests interleaved in a particular order. A sampling bug might appear only when a stop token is proposed inside a draft. Design the case that exercises the property instead of relying on an ordinary chat.

Deterministic sampling and batch invariance are separate promises. A seed controls the random draws. Batch invariance means a request’s output stays the same when its batch companions change, and that also depends on how the arithmetic is grouped. A seed alone does not make every numerical execution identical.

A good report states what the evidence establishes and names what it leaves open, such as task quality when only numbers were compared.
levels.2:
Checks work at several levels. Shape and index invariants catch structural mistakes. Comparing reference and optimized logits on shared prefixes tests the calculation. Greedy token equality tests the generation loop. Sampling-distribution checks test a stochastic sampler, and task-level evaluation tests whether the behavior is useful.

Passing a lower level does not establish the higher ones. A higher-level pass can also hide a lower-level bug that ordinary prompts never trigger.

For grammar constraints, an automaton tracks which continuations are allowed. At each step its state produces a token mask that shrinks the sampler’s legal set. Chunk boundaries, tokenization and stop behavior all affect whether that mask is right.

DeepInfer’s sampler contains both the verification logic for speculative drafts and the structured-output masking. Its offline example enables batch-invariant behavior on the NVIDIA path, so read the supported platform and configuration before generalizing from it.
levels.3:
A tolerance is a declared allowance for numerical difference, not a license to ignore unexplained mismatches. Choose one suited to the operation and the number format, and investigate patterns such as an error that jumps at a cache boundary. An approximation deserves its own, explicitly different quality contract, so that it never quietly weakens the promise of an exact rewrite.

Exercise adversarial boundaries: cache resets, zero- and one-token lengths where they are valid, maximum context, an end-of-sequence (EOS) token inside a draft, mixed request lengths, different co-batches and adapter switches. An incorrect fast path can look correct on every pleasant prompt.

For your own engine, keep an intentionally simple reference and compare layer outputs when a mismatch appears. Comparing final prose is too weak to debug attention or positional errors.

Quantization and approximate attention need task-level acceptance criteria. An exact-operation refactor should keep its exact contract and never drift into “looks about right.”

LESSONS.title: From a fast engine to a usable service
LESSONS.goal: Trace the work that surrounds a model calculation, and judge when splitting prefill and decode across machines pays for itself.
LESSONS.recall: Which parts of an online service live outside the engine loop?
LESSONS.predict: Can putting prefill and decode on separate workers make a small workload slower?
example: Fetching a cached prefix from a remote store takes 18 milliseconds and saves 10 milliseconds of prefill. Does the cache hit help this request?

Start by comparing the time added with the time saved. If the fetch cannot overlap with anything else, the request pays 18 milliseconds to avoid 10, and finishes 8 milliseconds later than it would have without the cache.

The fetch might overlap with other useful work, such as time the request would have spent queued anyway. It might also compete with other requests for network bandwidth. Either could change the answer, so time the fetch and the prefill separately on real traffic.
Report user-visible latency next to the hit rate. A higher hit rate means more prefixes were found, and it helps only when using them makes requests finish sooner.

questions.prompt: Putting prefill and decode on different workers creates a need to…
options: Move compatible attention state from the prefill worker to the decode worker
Tokenize the prompt again on the decode worker so it can rebuild the context
Run a separately trained model on each worker
questions.why: Decode continues from the attention state that prefill computed, so that state has to reach the decode worker intact and in a format it can use.
questions.hint: What did prefill produce that decode consumes?
option_feedback: Right: the decode worker needs the keys and values prefill computed, and they have to arrive complete and compatible.
Token IDs alone would force the decode worker to redo the prefill that the split was meant to move elsewhere.
Both stages run the same model; disaggregation changes where the work happens, and the weights stay the same.

questions.prompt: Which is a good first deployment goal for your fine-tuned model?
options: Reproduce a multi-stage production cluster like DeepSeek’s from the start
A correct single-engine baseline on a compatible engine, with measurements
Split every stage into its own service now so each can scale later
questions.why: A measured single-engine baseline gives every later change something to be compared against, and its failures are easy to locate.
questions.hint: Start where failure causes are easiest to isolate.
option_feedback: A production cluster adds handoffs and failure modes before you know which step of your workload is slow.
Right: a correct, measured baseline makes the cost and benefit of each later change visible.
Splitting early pays the handoff cost before any measurement shows that independent scaling is needed.

questions.prompt: Requests arrive faster than they complete, and the queue has no limit. What is the main risk?
options: Tail latency and memory use keep growing
Every user’s latency improves because the GPU never sits idle
Throughput keeps rising as the queue gets longer
questions.why: A queue adds no capacity. The excess work waits longer and longer while it keeps consuming memory.
questions.hint: Arrival rate can exceed completion rate.
option_feedback: Right: completion rate stays fixed, so the backlog and the wait at its end grow without bound.
A busy GPU finishes work at its usual rate; the requests behind the backlog still wait longer.
Throughput is capped by the engine’s completion rate, and a longer queue cannot raise that cap.

transfer: Describe a simple service for your fine-tuned model. Where does unfinished work live, and what should happen when a user cancels?
Identifies request queue and KV ownership
Includes model/tokenizer/adapter identity
Names cancellation/timeout handling

Requests first wait in a bounded queue and then run in a compatible engine. Each active request owns its working state, including its attention cache. The service records which base model, adapter and input format are in use. When a request completes or is cancelled, the service releases its slot and state once no consumer still needs them. I would get this simple path working before adding remote transfers or separately scaled stages.
LESSONS.takeaway: An engine becomes a usable service once queues, routing, state transfer and failure handling surround it.

levels.1:
A request spends only part of its life on the GPU.

A user types a question. Before any model calculation starts, a server has to receive it, check that the user may send it, turn the text into tokens, pick a worker, and perhaps hold the request until a slot frees up. When the model finishes, the token IDs are turned back into text and streamed to the user. Each of those steps can add delay, and each can fail.

That surrounding machinery is what turns an engine into a service. Keeping the two apart helps when you read a production architecture diagram. It also explains how an open-source engine can be fast and still fall short of something you could put in front of users. The DeepInfer README is explicit about which parts of DeepSeek’s internal service the release includes.

Large deployments can give each stage its own workers.

Prefill reads the whole known prompt in one pass. Decode then extends the answer one token at a time. The two load the hardware differently, so a large deployment can give each stage its own machines and its own scheduling. Running the stages apart like this is called disaggregation.

DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A describes a system that also gives multimodal encoding, the work of turning images into representations the model can read, a stage of its own. The stages still depend on one another. Decode cannot begin until it holds the numerical state that prefill produced.

Every split creates a handoff.

If one machine processes the prompt and another continues the answer, the attention state has to travel between them. The transfer uses network bandwidth, makes the request depend on a second machine, and opens one more place where something can go wrong.

For a large or uneven workload, scaling prompt work and answer work independently can repay those costs. A small workload may run better with both stages on one machine. Measurements of your own traffic are what settle which case you are in.

Queues hold work without adding capacity.

When requests arrive faster than the engine completes them, the unfinished ones pile up. If the queue may grow without limit, requests at the back wait longer and longer. A service needs a policy that says how much work to admit, how long a request may wait, and what happens when either limit is reached.

Requests also end early. A user closes the tab, or a timeout fires. The service has to notice and release that request’s memory and scheduler slot, or abandoned work keeps occupying space that live requests need.

Start with a system you can explain.

For a first service around your fine-tuned model, use one compatible engine and a workload that resembles your real traffic. Confirm that it loads the model you intended and behaves as expected. Then measure which step of the request’s journey is slow, before you copy an architecture built for a far larger load.
levels.2:
Draw the full path of one request: request → format and tokenize → queue → prefill → transfer state → decode → detokenize and stream. Add prefix-cache lookup, admission control and cancellation as side branches. Every arrow is a place where latency can accumulate or a failure can occur.

Then label who owns state at each point. The queue owns pending requests. A running engine owns each request’s attention state. A transfer protocol has to define the moment another worker takes over, and streaming has to deliver output in order from a single owner. Add a boundary only when you can say what crosses it and what happens if the crossing fails.

The DeepSeek Q&A describes a larger encode, prefill and decode system with a separate store for cached state. Read its diagrams as a description of DeepSeek’s own service. The README is the authority on what the public release lets you run.

Independent scaling helps when prompt work and output work grow at different rates. The state transfer then has to fit inside the network budget and meet the reliability the product needs.
levels.3:
A distributed design is also a failure-handling design. When a worker disappears mid-request, you have to decide whether the request fails, retries from scratch, or resumes elsewhere. Resuming needs a complete, compatible copy of the state and one clear owner of the output that follows. Mistakes here produce wrong answers as well as slow ones.

Decide overload behavior on purpose. The service can reject new work, queue it with a deadline, or admit less work under an explicit product contract. An unbounded queue converts a capacity shortfall into extreme tail latency.

Cancellation must free cache space and scheduler slots. Migration needs complete state and a single owner of further output. Cache reuse must check the model, the adapter and any access boundaries, so that a cached prefix serves only requests that run the same model and are allowed to see it.

Begin your own service with one compatible engine and a fixed, representative workload. Put observability and correctness checks in place before you experiment with distributed layouts.

LESSONS.title: Read DeepInfer without getting lost
LESSONS.goal: Follow one request through DeepInfer before studying any single optimization.
LESSONS.recall: What evidence separates an engine feature from a production service feature?
LESSONS.predict: Will reading every kernel before the request loop give you the clearest first map?
example: You find an output clone inside the generation loop. How do you decide whether it is needed?

Find out what the raw output points to. Here, the nearby code and comment concern storage that a later engine step can release or reuse. Appending the object to a list would only keep a reference to that storage, and the contents behind a reference can change.
Trace when the consumer reads the saved result and when the producer can overwrite the buffer behind it. If those moments can overlap, the copy is what keeps the two lifetimes apart.

Before removing it, write a test that saves one output, forces the engine to reuse the buffer, and then reads the saved output again. Any replacement has to keep that earlier value intact, either by copying or through an ownership protocol you can prove.

questions.prompt: What is the best first route through the repository?
options: Start with an example and follow one request through to its results.
Read every file in directory order, so nothing is missed, before tracing a request.
Start from the most optimized kernels, since they dominate the benchmark results.
questions.why: Following one request ties every file you open to behavior you can observe, so the map you build stays connected.
questions.hint: Follow one request, not the directory tree.
option_feedback: Right: one traced request shows how the pieces cooperate, and each file answers part of a question you already have.
Reading in directory order covers files without showing how they connect, so the details rarely add up to a map.
Kernels matter for speed, but without the request loop you cannot tell when they run or what they receive.

questions.prompt: Why should a code link in your notes pin a commit?
options: It guarantees that the linked code is correct
It identifies the exact revision your explanation describes
It keeps the link working if the repository is renamed
questions.why: A link to main shows whatever main holds later. A pinned commit shows a future reader the same code you read.
questions.hint: What will a future reader actually see?
option_feedback: A pinned commit can contain bugs; pinning records which code you read and says nothing about its correctness.
Right: the explanation stays tied to the code it was written about, even after main changes.
Renames are handled by redirects, if at all; the point of pinning is that the file contents stay fixed.

questions.prompt: An output is cloned just before the engine may reuse its buffers. What should you check before calling the clone waste?
options: Whether a saved result would change after the buffer is reused
Whether the optimizer state is updated during inference
Whether the clone makes the output tensor larger
questions.why: If the consumer reads after the producer has overwritten the buffer, removing the copy lets it read changed data.
questions.hint: Relate the copy to async reuse.
option_feedback: Right: the clone may be what keeps the saved result’s lifetime separate from the reused buffer’s.
Inference does not run an optimizer, so optimizer state cannot explain a copy in the generation loop.
A clone has the same shape and size as its source; the question is whether its values stay fixed.

transfer: Trace one request through DeepInfer in a few sentences. Name one property you would test at a specific boundary.
Traces entrypoint to scheduling to execution to sampling
Names request-owned state
Names an observable invariant

The example creates the model and calls generation. The entry point admits the requests, then repeatedly asks the engine to schedule and execute work. Model execution produces the values that sampling uses, and result handling updates each request and collects its outputs. Each request keeps its own state. At the output-collection boundary, I would test that an output saved earlier stays unchanged after a later step reuses the producer’s buffer.
LESSONS.takeaway: Build your map by following one request, then study one responsibility at a time.

activity.title: Trace one request and name the promise at one boundary.
activity.intro: Open the pinned entry point below. Start at generate, follow the loop that collects outputs, and find where an output is copied before it is kept. The task covers one small path through the engine.

fields.label: In your own words, what enters and leaves this path?
fields.placeholder: The caller provides… The engine repeatedly… The caller eventually receives…

fields.label: Choose one boundary and state what must stay true.
fields.placeholder: At the point where an output is saved, it must…

fields.label: What small test would expose a violation?
fields.placeholder: Produce one result, then… Read it again and compare…

compare: Follow the actual function calls and the values they save. A function’s name alone does not tell you its responsibility.
One useful promise is that a result kept for the caller stays unchanged after the engine reuses temporary storage.
Use outputs you can tell apart, and read the first saved value again after a later engine step. Comparing shapes alone would miss a changed value.
activity.example: For the output-copy boundary, I would create an output containing token 7, let the collector save it, then reuse the producer’s storage for token 9. The saved first output should still contain 7. This checks one lifetime promise; it does not prove every engine path correct.

levels.1:
You can understand one path through a repository before you understand every file.

Opening a large engine repository can feel like walking into the middle of a conversation. There are kernels, worker processes, configuration flags, and several different objects that each represent a request. Reading the files in alphabetical order rarely shows how these pieces cooperate.

A better start is one concrete question: what happens when this example asks the model for a response? Follow that request from input to output, and let each function you meet answer a smaller part of the question.

Begin with the example’s inputs.

Open examples/offline_inference.py. Find where it chooses a model, sets how many devices take part, creates the engine and asks for outputs. Most of the options can wait. Write down what the example passes into generation and what it expects to get back.

Find the public entry point.

Next, open deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py. Its generation method admits requests and then runs a loop until they finish. Follow the call that adds a request, and then the loop that collects its outputs.

As you read, ask where each request’s identity comes from, which state belongs to it, and how its results come back in the right order. Those questions tie the code to the engine responsibilities you already know.

Then follow one execution step.

In deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py, find the step method, the scheduling call, the asynchronous execution and the result handling. The scheduler picks the work, model execution performs it, and post-processing updates each request’s state. Trace that sequence once before you open any kernel.

Choose one detail to investigate.

In the entry point, output objects are cloned before the next step can reuse their underlying storage. A copy on a hot path looks like an easy saving. The nearby comment ties this one to storage a later step can reuse, which makes it a clue about data lifetime before it is a candidate for deletion.

You could instead follow sampling into sampler.py and separate ordinary token selection from the verification of draft tokens. Whichever detail you pick, find the inputs it receives and the outputs it owns.

Keep track of what kind of claim each line of your notes is: something you saw in the code, something the authors report, or something you inferred. The source links in this course pin a specific commit, so a colleague can open exactly the code you read.
levels.2:
For each call you follow, write one sentence: “This function receives ___, decides or calculates ___, and returns or changes ___.” If you cannot complete the sentence, follow that one dependency and stop there. The reading stays bounded, and the gaps show you where a test could attach.

A single vertical path gives you a map for later exploration. It does not show that you have inspected every configuration or execution branch.

  • examples/offline_inference.py: find the EP, DP and CP arguments (expert, data and context parallelism) and the place where the model is created.
  • deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py: follow generate → _add_request → _run_engine, and notice how results are ordered and outputs cloned.
  • deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py: find step, then scheduling, asynchronous execution and post_process.
  • deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sampler.py: tell apart the logits, the grammar mask and draft verification.
  • schedule_mtp_varlen.py: find the cumulative confidence, the top-budget selection and the per-sequence query lengths.

Leave the flags alone at first. Predict which function should run, then confirm it with a trace or a tiny test.
levels.3:
A good first change to an engine is often small: a missing boundary test, a loader fix, or a correction to a benchmark that measured the wrong thing. Start from an observation you can reproduce and an invariant you can check. The value of a contribution has little to do with how many kernel lines it touches.

Confidence scheduling is one seam worth trying. Identify its inputs and their valid ranges, the mandatory target-token budget, how ties are broken, and how each selection stays a prefix of the draft. Then write a small reference computation and compare it with the implementation.

The browser lab in this course reduces selection to expected accepted drafts under a fixed budget. The real engine also handles target slots, hardware profiles and asynchronous metadata. Use the lab to see the idea, and treat the engine code as the authority on what actually runs.

LESSONS.title: Your fine-tuned model is more than a weights file
LESSONS.goal: Know which files and settings you need to reproduce the model you fine-tuned.
LESSONS.recall: Why can the wrong tokenizer make correct weights behave incorrectly?
LESSONS.predict: If two checkpoints share an architecture name, can you apply the same LoRA adapter to either base revision?
example: An adapter trained on base revision R1 loads on R2 without a shape error. Have you established that it is the model you trained?

A clean load shows that some structural expectations were met. It does not show that R2 contains the base values the adapter was trained to modify, because matching dimensions leave that question open.
Recover the intended base revision and the adapter configuration from the training record. Keep the tokenizer, the custom prompt format and the stop settings consistent with training too.

Load that exact combination in a reference implementation. Feed a deployment path the same tokenized inputs and compare, then check the behavior you want on a separate evaluation set. That establishes far more than a successful load.

questions.prompt: A LoRA adapter is usually…
options: A replacement tokenizer trained for the new task
A learned update that needs a compatible base model
A complete copy of the fine-tuned weights
questions.why: The adapter modifies selected base operations and usually omits the base weights, so it can only run on top of a compatible base.
questions.hint: Where are the original large matrices?
option_feedback: LoRA trains changes to weight matrices; the tokenizer comes from the base model and stays the same.
Right: the adapter stores a small update, and the large base matrices have to come from the matching base model.
A merged checkpoint is a full copy, but a saved LoRA adapter usually holds only the low-rank update.

questions.prompt: What should you check first when choosing an engine for your model?
options: Whether its supported-model list includes a similarly named model
The exact architecture, engine version, and support for your artifacts and adapter
Whether it loads the checkpoint without raising an error
questions.why: Support depends on the specific architecture and the implementation features you use, and neither a similar name nor a clean load establishes it.
questions.hint: A friendly model name is not an execution contract.
option_feedback: Model families share names across different architectures and revisions, so a name match is weak evidence.
Right: support is defined per architecture, version and feature, such as adapter serving or a numerical format.
A checkpoint can load without errors while running the wrong base or ignoring part of the configuration.

questions.prompt: Merged and unmerged LoRA give slightly different BF16 logits. What is the first interpretation to test?
options: Proof that the adapter was applied incorrectly
Rounding from a different operation order; compare against a declared tolerance and task checks
Evidence that merging changed the model’s architecture
questions.why: The two routes are equal in real-number algebra, but finite-precision arithmetic rounds them in a different order.
questions.hint: Where does each route round its intermediate results?
option_feedback: A small difference is expected from rounding; an incorrect adapter would usually show up as larger or task-level differences.
Right: BF16 rounds each intermediate result, so reordering the operations can shift the last digits.
Merging folds the update into existing matrices; the layers and their arrangement stay the same.

transfer: What would you save alongside a LoRA adapter so another person could run the model you actually fine-tuned?
Pins base and adapter identity
Includes tokenizer/prompt/stop/config
Includes precision, versions and evaluation fixture

I would record the exact base revision and save the adapter’s configuration and learned values. I would include the model configuration, the correct tokenizer, the input format used in training and the stop-token rules. Numerical precision, quantization settings and library versions also affect whether someone can reproduce the model. Finally, I would keep fixed tokenized inputs and a held-out evaluation record, so a new loader or engine has something concrete to be compared against.
LESSONS.takeaway: A usable fine-tuned model includes its exact base, its learned update, its tokenizer and input format, and the settings it ran with.

activity.title: Write down which model you intend to run.
activity.intro: Use a model you have fine-tuned, or one you plan to fine-tune. If a detail is not decided yet, write “not chosen yet.” Gaps are easier to fill now than after the training files are gone. These notes stay in this browser and can be exported with your progress.

fields.label: Exact base model and saved revision
fields.placeholder: Repository or local checkpoint, plus its immutable revision. “Latest” is not an exact version.

fields.label: Adapter or merged checkpoint, and its configuration
fields.placeholder: Saved weights, target modules, adapter settings, and the base version they were trained with.

fields.label: Tokenizer, input format, and stop rules
fields.placeholder: Tokenizer revision, training prompt format or template, special tokens, and when generation should stop.

fields.label: A small reference example to save
fields.placeholder: One fixed formatted input, its token IDs, generation settings, and a held-out task you care about.

compare: Another person needs the intended base version and adapter configuration as well as the learned adapter numbers.
Matching array dimensions does not prove that a different base contains the intended learned values.
The tokenizer, training input pattern, special tokens, and stop rules are part of reproducing the intended model.
An unchosen detail is a useful open question. Filling in a field does not verify that the files on disk match the note.
activity.example: For a planned LoRA deployment, I would record an immutable base revision, the adapter weights and configuration, the tokenizer revision, the exact completion format used during training, and stop tokens. I would save a fixed formatted input and its token IDs, then establish the adapted reference before trying a new engine.

levels.1:
A weights file is only part of the model you trained.

Suppose you fine-tune a base model and want to run the result in an inference engine. It is tempting to think a weights file finishes the job. The engine also needs to know what those numbers mean, and how inputs were represented while the model learned them.

First, the engine must support the model’s architecture, the arrangement of layers and calculations that its configuration describes. Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers inside that arrangement and leaves the arrangement itself alone. An engine that cannot execute the base model cannot execute your tuned version either.

An adapter may contain only the change.

With LoRA, a common fine-tuning method, you train a compact update attached to selected matrices of the base model. The saved adapter usually leaves out the base weights themselves. To run it you need the compatible base, the adapter’s configuration and its learned values.

Two revisions of a base model can share every dimension and still hold different learned numbers. An adapter trained on one may load onto the other without a shape error, and the clean load says nothing about whether it now computes what you trained.

The text format is part of what the model learned.

A tokenizer assigns IDs to pieces of text and to special markers. A chat template arranges messages and roles into the token sequence a chat-trained model expects to see. A completion model may instead expect whatever custom format you used during training.

Change any of these and behavior can shift while every weight loads cleanly. Keep the intended tokenizer, input format and stop-token rules with the model files.

Record enough to rebuild the same computation.

An artifact manifest is a short record of the pieces you used: the exact base revision, the adapter or merged weights, the model configuration, the tokenizer and format, the numerical precision and the relevant library versions. A name like “latest base” points somewhere new each time the base is updated, so record an immutable revision.

You can serve an adapter next to its supported base, or, where the tooling allows, merge its update into a full set of weights. Each route needs its own checks, especially once reduced precision or quantization is involved.

Before optimizing anything, load the intended combination in a reference implementation and save a few fixed inputs with their expected scores or task results. When an engine later appears to run the model, those saved cases give you something concrete to compare against.
levels.2:
LoRA represents a large update as the product of two small matrices. You can apply that product during execution, or multiply it into the base weight ahead of time. In exact real-number arithmetic the two routes give the same result.

For a weight W, ordinary LoRA uses W′=W+sBA, where A and B have a small inner rank and s is a scaling factor. For a row-vector input, the merged route computes x(W+sBA)ᵀ and the unmerged route computes xWᵀ+s(xAᵀ)Bᵀ.

Computers round intermediate results, and the two routes round in a different order, so their outputs can differ slightly. Judge that difference against a stated numerical tolerance and a task check. Equal algebra does not promise bitwise-equal outputs in every numeric format.

That leaves two deployment choices. You can serve a supported adapter alongside its exact base, or merge the update into a compatible floating-point model and save a complete checkpoint. The PEFT LoRA reference and vLLM’s LoRA serving guide describe what each supports; check them for your version, because quantized models and adapter variants can carry extra restrictions.
levels.3:
The identity that matters for loading also matters for caching. An adapter changes the intermediate attention state. If you switch adapters and reuse state computed under the earlier one, the engine computes a hybrid that matches neither model. Test adapter switches as well as first loads, and make adapter identity part of the cache compatibility check.

A manifest worth keeping records the following.

  • Base model ID and immutable revision
  • A hash of the architecture and configuration
  • Tokenizer and template identity
  • Adapter target modules, rank and scaling
  • Precision and quantization method
  • Library versions and context settings
  • The revision of the evaluation dataset

Mutable names are not enough provenance on their own. Use a fixed held-out set with known desired behavior to compare the base model, the adapted reference and the engine’s output. Check token IDs before logits, since a formatting mismatch spoils every later comparison. If your base was trained as a completion model, do not invent a chat template that your fine-tuning never used.

LESSONS.title: What a cache must remember
LESSONS.goal: Read one cache slice, predict what it removes, and repair it using actual model scores.
LESSONS.recall: Which numerical comparison shows that a cache is correct?
LESSONS.predict: If a cache accidentally drops its first key/value, will matching tensor shapes detect it?
example: We process input IDs [1, 4]. These numbers name tokens; the keys and values saved in the cache are computed from them.
The first input creates the entry at position 0. With only one entry, attention gives it all of the weight, and the cached path and the full-prefix reference use the same information.

The second input adds an entry at position 1. Starting the read at 0 keeps both entries. Attention splits its weight between the two saved values, and the cached scores still agree with the reference.

Now change only the read boundary, to 1. Position 0 is still stored, but attention no longer receives it, so the remaining entry gets all of the weight. Inspect one next-token score to see what the missing contribution does to the numbers.

questions.prompt: The cache contains entries at positions 0 and 1. What does cache.values[1:] pass to attention?
questions.why: The slice begins at index 1 and continues to the end. It leaves position 0 out of the values passed to attention, even though that entry still exists in the cache.
questions.hint: Python starts counting at zero. The number before the colon is the first included position.
option_feedback: That would be [0:]; the number before the colon is the first position included.
Right: [1:] starts at index 1 and runs to the end, so position 0 stays in the cache but never reaches attention.
Position 0 is exactly the entry the slice skips; selecting only it would need [0:1].

questions.prompt: A wrong cache offset can leave every shape unchanged. Which check is needed?
options: Compare actual logits against the full-prefix reference
questions.why: The wrong read has the right dimensions, so only the values, compared against a reference that recomputes the full prefix, expose it.
questions.hint: A structurally valid wrong result is still wrong.
option_feedback: Both slices still hold one key and one value each, so a length check passes on the broken read.
Right: the full-prefix reference shows which scores the cached path should have produced, entry by entry.
Speed says nothing about which history attention read; a wrong cache can be just as fast.

questions.prompt: After you vectorize the engine, what should happen to the simple scalar reference?
options: Be retained as a small numerical oracle
questions.why: A simple, independent implementation keeps catching mistakes that the optimized path introduces.
questions.hint: What makes later changes safe to inspect?
option_feedback: Right: a small, slow, obviously correct version is the oracle each optimization is compared against.
The scalar loop is too slow to serve; its value is as a check, while the vectorized code does the real work.
Fluent-looking text can hide changed scores, and a tiny random-weight model never produces fluent text anyway.

transfer: Your teammate says: “The keys and values still have equal lengths, so starting the cache read at 1 is safe.” Explain what the code actually omits, how that changes the calculation, and what comparison supports your repair.
Names the omitted cache position and its contribution
Connects the changed visible values to changed model scores
Repairs the read boundary and compares with the same full-prefix reference

With two saved positions, starting at 1 leaves position 0 out of both slices. Equal slice lengths only show that the keys and values are still paired; they say nothing about whether the intended history is present. Attention then mixes only the remaining value, so the later calculations can produce different next-token scores. Starting at 0 restores both positions. I would compare cached and full-prefix scores on the same inputs, including the second position, where this bug first appears. Matching scores support the repair. They say nothing about speed.
LESSONS.takeaway: A cache has to preserve the right history; two arrays with matching lengths can still be missing an entry.

activity.title: Repair the highlighted cache read.
activity.intro: The cache now has positions 0 and 1. Change the highlighted start value, predict which entries attention will receive, and run the selected branch of the actual CPU engine.

levels.1:
A cache lets the engine skip recomputing earlier tokens, but attention still has to read every piece of history it needs. Below, you will trace two token positions through the code above, then repair a one-line change that quietly drops part of that history.

Read the slice before running the model.

Python counts positions from zero. With two saved entries, [0:] selects positions 0 and 1, and [1:] selects only position 1. The colon means “from here to the end.” The stored arrays keep their full size; the slice decides which entries the calculation receives.

What is actually stored?

Each saved entry holds a key and a value, two vectors of numbers computed from a token and its position. The query, named q in the code, comes from the current token. Attention compares the query with each visible key and uses the resulting weights to mix the matching values.

Leave an entry out of the read and its contribution to that mixture disappears. The rest of the model then works from a different mixture and produces different next-token scores. The key and value slices can still have equal lengths while the calculation is wrong.

Why does starting at position 1 change the scores?

That is the question to answer once the second input arrives. In “See an example,” watch the actual entries and attention weights at each position. In “Try it,” change the highlighted value, predict which entries remain, and run your version. Then explain why your repair is justified.

The small model uses random weights and numbered tokens, so its output will never read as fluent language. It is there to make each step of the calculation visible.
levels.2:
The property to check is that two implementations, given the same sequence, calculate the same next-token scores within a chosen tolerance. Generated text is a blunter debugging signal, because one changed token changes every input after it.

For a scheduler, compare each request against its own independent generation. Include requests that finish early and a new request that takes over a freed slot.

Use the code viewer to inspect attention, full_logits and cached_step. Predict each tensor’s shape, then trace one prompt token by token. The reference recomputes the full prefix at every step, while the cached path keeps the keys and values it has already computed.

The broken-read experiment in “Try it” switches on a deliberately wrong cache boundary. Predict the first prefix where the two paths diverge, run it, then find the one-line cause. The result table should show the mismatch.

The tests also compare interleaved request states, and explicit against merged low-rank updates to the output head. Those updates are constructed examples. They are not trained adapters, and the tiny engine does not load PEFT checkpoints.
levels.3:
Vectorizing the arithmetic changes how work is executed. Paging the cache changes how state is stored and addressed. Chunking prefill changes how known inputs are divided into units of work. Try these one at a time at first, so that a failure points to the single new mechanism that caused it.

  • Add an explicit maximum-context policy that says whether the engine rejects or truncates. Silently changing what attention sees is a behavior change.
  • Add a scheduler that admits a waiting request after another finishes. Keep the caches separate and compare every request with its independent generation.
  • Port the matrix operations to NumPy or PyTorch, and keep the reference as the oracle.
  • Only then try chunked prefill or paged storage, with tests at page boundaries.

Compare every extension with the independent reference. Include early finishes, a new request taking over a freed slot, and cases on both sides of a storage boundary. A scheduler that organizes requests still runs them one matrix operation at a time until you fuse them, so measure the work the implementation actually performs.

LESSONS.title: Serve your first real fine-tuned model
LESSONS.goal: Move your fine-tuned model into a compatible engine and check that it still behaves as intended.
LESSONS.recall: What must match between training-time prompt formatting and inference?
LESSONS.predict: If the server returns HTTP 200, do you know it is using your adapter?
example: The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and reports your adapter’s name. What further evidence would show that it runs your adapted model?
Confirm the actual base and adapter artifacts the engine loaded. A label in the response can name the intended configuration without proving which learned values are in memory.

Compare fixed inputs against the adapted reference. Include a held-out task where the adapted model behaves noticeably differently from the base, and compare numerical predictions where the engine exposes them.
Once that behavior is established, test concurrent requests, limits and restart or reload behavior. These service checks add to the model comparison and cannot stand in for it.

questions.prompt: A successful HTTP response proves…
options: The endpoint answered; model identity and behavior still need their own checks.
The intended weights and adapter were loaded, since a loading error would have failed the request.
Outputs will not change when other requests share the batch.
questions.why: A successful response shows that transport worked. Whether the intended model ran correctly is a separate question with its own evidence.
questions.hint: Match the observation to what it can establish.
option_feedback: Right: a 200 status reports that a response was delivered, and nothing about which weights produced it.
Many servers fall back to the base model or ignore an unknown adapter and still return 200.
Batch composition is a property of the engine’s numerics and scheduling; the status code reports none of it.

questions.prompt: Before comparing the reference with an engine, what should you hold fixed?
options: Prompt token IDs, model artifacts and generation settings
The visible question text, letting each system format it its own way
The maximum output length, since it causes most of the differences
questions.why: If the tokenizer or template differs, the two systems run different token sequences and the comparison mixes formatting with execution.
questions.hint: Compare the same numerical task.
option_feedback: Right: with identical token IDs, artifacts and settings, a remaining difference points at the engine.
The same visible text can become different token sequences under different templates, which confounds the comparison.
Output length matters, but formatting, artifacts and sampling settings can change results even at equal length.

questions.prompt: What is the safest first speed experiment?
options: Change precision, batching and the tokenizer together to find the best combination quickly
Change one measured bottleneck while keeping the reference checks and workload fixed
Raise concurrency until the server fails, then back off
questions.why: Changing one measured thing against a fixed reference and workload makes any improvement or regression attributable to that change.
questions.hint: Which comparison could explain the result?
option_feedback: With three changes at once, a speedup or a quality loss cannot be traced to any one of them.
Right: a single change, measured on the same workload with the same checks, has one possible cause.
Finding the failure point is a stress test; it says nothing about which change would make the service faster.

transfer: Describe your first experiment moving a fine-tuned model into an inference engine. How will you tell what caused a difference?
Names architecture/artifacts and compatible engine
Defines reference and quality criteria
Defines workload and latency/throughput measurements

I would start with the exact base, adapter, configuration, tokenizer and training-time input format in a direct reference implementation. I would save fixed token IDs, generation settings and held-out task results. Then I would pick an engine whose documentation supports that architecture and adapter path, and compare it on the same inputs. I would test quantization separately, so that any observed difference can be traced to one change.
LESSONS.takeaway: Establish the intended model in a reference path, then change one execution variable at a time.

activity.title: Plan the first reference-to-engine comparison.
activity.intro: Bring forward the model record from the previous lesson. Choose one compatible engine and one small comparison you could run first. Keep the first experiment offline, so that endpoint behavior cannot hide a model or input mismatch.

source.label: Check official vLLM model support as one starting point

fields.label: Engine, version, and support evidence
fields.placeholder: Which exact architecture and adapter path are supported? Link the documentation you checked and note unresolved limits.

fields.label: Fixed inputs and reference command or procedure

Give both paths the same token IDs and generation rules. Identical visible text can become different inputs under different formatting.
A direct numerical comparison and a held-out task answer different questions. If only controlled generation is available, state that weaker boundary.
Establish the adapted reference before changing the engine. Evaluate quantization separately, then test service behavior after offline correctness.

I would select an engine version whose documentation supports that architecture and adapter path, then compare the same inputs and stop rules.
